entries.dffb9128f721c236755e54b5f4b7cd70fc9970d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv89"/><title type="x-ms">Ecclesiastes</title> <div sID="gen14824" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14825" type="x-p"/> We are still among Solomon's happy men, his happy servants, that <hi type="italic">stood continually before him to hear his wisdom;</hi> and they are the choicest of all the dictates of his wisdom, such as were more immediately given by divine inspiration, that are here transmitted to us, not to be heard, as by them, but once, and then liable to be mistaken or forgotten, and by repetition to lose their beauty, but to be read, reviewed, revolved, and had in everlasting remembrance. The account we have of Solomon's apostasy from God, in the latter end of his reign (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.1">1 Kings xi. 1</reference>), is the tragical part of his story; we may suppose that he spoke his <hi type="italic">Proverbs</hi> in the prime of his time, while he kept his integrity, but delivered his <hi type="italic">Ecclesiastes</hi> when he had grown old (for of the burdens and decays of age he speaks feelingly <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1-Eccl.12.14">ch. xii.</reference>), and was, by the grace of God, recovered from his backslidings. There he dictated his observations; here he wrote his own experiences; this is what days speak, and wisdom which the multitude of years teaches. The title of the book and the penman we shall meet with in the <div eID="gen14825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14826" type="x-p"/> I. That it is a sermon, a sermon in print; the text is (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.2">ch. i. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Vanity of vanities, all is vanity;</hi> that is the doctrine too; it is proved at large by many arguments and an induction of particulars, and divers objections are answered, and in the close we have the use and application of all, by way of exhortation, to <hi type="italic">remember our Creator,</hi> to <hi type="italic">fear him,</hi> and to <hi type="italic">keep his commandments.</hi> There are indeed many things in this book which are dark and hard to be understood, and some things which men of corrupt minds <hi type="italic">wrest to their own destruction,</hi> for want of distinguishing between Solomon's arguments and the objections of atheists and epicures; but there is enough easy and plain to convince us (if we will admit the conviction) of the vanity of the world, and its utter insufficiency to make us happy, the vileness of sin, and its certain tendency to make us miserable, and of the wisdom of being religious, and the solid comfort and satisfaction that are to be had in doing our duty both to God and man. This should be intended in every sermon, and that is a good sermon by which these points are in any measure gained. II. That it is a penitential sermon, as some of David's psalms are penitential psalms; it is a recantation-sermon, in which the preacher sadly laments his own folly and mistake, in promising himself satisfaction in the things of this world, and even in the forbidden pleasures of sense, which now he finds more bitter than death. His fall is a proof of the weakness of man's nature: <hi type="italic">Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom,</hi> nor say, "I shall never be such a fool as to do so and so," when Solomon himself, the wisest of men, played the fool so egregiously; nor <hi type="italic">let the rich man glory in his riches,</hi> since Solomon's wealth was so great a snare to him, and did him a great deal more hurt than Job's poverty did him. His recovery is a proof of the power of God's grace, in bringing one back to God that has gone so far from him; it is a proof too of the riches of God's mercy in accepting him notwithstanding the many aggravations of his sin, pursuant to the promise made to David, that if his children should commit iniquity they should be corrected, but not abandoned and disinherited, <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.14-2Sam.7.15">2 Sam. vii. 14, 15</reference>. Let him therefore that thinks he stands take heed lest he fall; and let him that has fallen make haste to get up again, and not despair either of assistance or acceptance therein. III. That it is a practical profitable sermon. Solomon, being brought to repentance, resolves, like his father, to teach transgressors God's way (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.13">Ps. li. 13</reference>) and to give warning to all to take heed of splitting upon those rocks which had been fatal to him; and these were fruits meet for repentance. The fundamental error of the children of men, and that which is at the bottom of all their departures from God, is the same with that of our first parents, hoping to be as gods by entertaining themselves with that which seems good for food, pleasant to the eyes, and desirable to make one wise. Now the scope of this book is to show that this is a great mistake, that our happiness consists not in being as gods to ourselves, to have what we will and do what we will, but in having him that made us to be a God to us. The moral philosophers disputed much about man's felicity, or chief good. Various opinions they had about it; but Solomon, in this book, determines the question, and assures us that to fear God and to keep his commandments is the whole of man. He tried what satisfaction might be found in the wealth of the world and the pleasures of sense, and at last pronounced all vanity and vexation; yet multitudes will not take his word, but will make the same dangerous experiment, and it proves fatal to them. He, 1. Shows the vanity of those things in which men commonly look for happiness, as human learning and policy, sensual delight, honour and power, riches and great possessions. And then, 2. He prescribes remedies against the vexation of spirit that attends them. Though we cannot cure them of their vanity, we may prevent the trouble they give us, by sitting loose to them, enjoying them comfortable, but laying our expectations low from them, and acquiescing in the will of God concerning us in every event, especially by remembering God in the days of our youth, and continuing in his fear and service all our days, with an eye to the judgment to come. <div eID="gen14826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14827" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14828" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The inscription, or title of the book, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The general doctrine of the vanity of the creature laid down (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.2">ver. 2</reference>) and explained, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.3">ver. 3</reference>. III. The proof of this doctrine, taken, 1. From the shortness of human life and the multitude of births and burials in this life, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">ver. 4</reference>. 2. From the inconstant nature, and constant revolutions, of all the creatures, and the perpetual flux and reflux they are in, the sun, wind, and water, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.5-Eccl.1.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. 3. From the abundant toil man has about them and the little satisfaction he has in them, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">ver. 8</reference>. 4. From the return of the same things again, which shows the end of all perfection, and that the stock is exhausted, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9-Eccl.1.10">ver. 9, 10</reference>. 5. From the oblivion to which all things are condemned, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.11">ver. 11</reference>. IV. The first instance of the vanity of man's knowledge, and all the parts of learning, especially natural philosophy and politics. Observe, 1. The trial Solomon made of these, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12-Eccl.1.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.16">16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">17</reference>. 2. His judgment of them, that all is vanity, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.14">ver. 14</reference>. For, (1.) There is labour in getting knowledge, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">ver. 13</reference>. (2.) There is little good to be done with it, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">ver. 15</reference>. (3.) There is no satisfaction in it, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.18">ver. 18</reference>. And, if this is vanity and vexation, all other things in this world, being much inferior to it in dignity and worth, must needs be so too. A great scholar cannot be happy unless he be a true saint. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv89"/> <div eID="gen14828" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14827" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vanity of the World.</title> <div sID="gen14829" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all <hi type="italic">is</hi> vanity. <hi type="super">3</hi> What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun? <div eID="gen14829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14830" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. An account of the penman of this book; it was Solomon, for no other son of David was king of Jerusalem; but he conceals his name <hi type="italic">Solomon, peaceable,</hi> because by his sin he had brought trouble upon himself and his kingdom, had broken his peace with God and lost the peace of his conscience, and therefore was no more worthy of that name. Call me not <hi type="italic">Solomon,</hi> call me <hi type="italic">Marah,</hi> for, <hi type="italic">behold, for peace I had great bitterness.</hi> But he calls himself, <div eID="gen14830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14831" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">The preacher,</hi> which intimates his present character. He is <hi type="italic">Koheleth,</hi> which comes from a word which signifies <hi type="italic">to gather;</hi> but it is of a feminine termination, by which perhaps Solomon intends to upbraid himself with his effeminacy, which contributed more than any thing to his apostasy; for it was to please his wives that he set up idols, <reference osisRef="Neh.13.26">Neh. xiii. 26</reference>. Or the word <hi type="italic">soul</hi> must be understood, and so <hi type="italic">Koheleth</hi> is, <div eID="gen14831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14832" type="x-p"/> (1.) A <hi type="italic">penitent soul,</hi> or one <hi type="italic">gathered,</hi> one that had rambled and gone astray like a lost sheep, but was now reduced, gathered in from his wanderings, gathered home to his duty, and come at length to himself. The spirit that was dissipated after a thousand vanities is now collected and made to centre in God. Divine grace can make great sinners great converts, and renew even those to repentance who, <hi type="italic">after they had known the way of righteousness, turned aside from it,</hi> and <hi type="italic">heal their backslidings,</hi> though it is a difficult case. It is only the penitent soul that God will accept, the heart that is broken, not the head that is bowed down like a bulrush only for a day, David's repentance, not Ahab's. And it is only the gathered soul that is the penitent soul, that comes back from its by-paths, that no longer <hi type="italic">scatters its way to the strangers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.13">Jer. iii. 13</reference>), but is <hi type="italic">united to fear God's name. Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth will speak,</hi> and therefore we have here the words of the penitent, and those published. If eminent professors of religion fall into gross sin, they are concerned, for the honour of God and the repairing of the damage they have done to his kingdom, openly to testify their repentance, that the antidote may be administered as extensively as the poison. <div eID="gen14832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14833" type="x-p"/> (2.) A <hi type="italic">preaching soul,</hi> or one <hi type="italic">gathering.</hi> Being himself <hi type="italic">gathered</hi> to the congregation of saints, out of which he had by his sin thrown himself, and being reconciled to the church, he endeavours to gather others to it that had gone astray like him, and perhaps were led astray by his example. He that has done any thing to seduce his brother ought to do all he can to restore him. Perhaps Solomon called together a congregation of his people, as he had done at the dedication of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.2">1 Kings viii. 2</reference>), so now at the rededicating of himself. In that assembly he presided as the people's mouth to God in prayer (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12">v. 12</reference>); in this as God's mouth to them in preaching. God by his Spirit made him a preacher, in token of his being reconciled to him; a commission is a tacit pardon. Christ sufficiently testifies his forgiving Peter by committing his lambs and sheep to his trust. Observe, Penitents should be preachers; those that have taken warning themselves to turn and live should give warning to others not to go on and die. <hi type="italic">When thou art converted strengthen thy brethren.</hi> Preachers must be preaching <hi type="italic">souls,</hi> for that only is likely to reach to the heart that comes from the heart. Paul served God <hi type="italic">with his spirit in the gospel of his Son,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.9">Rom. i. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen14833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14834" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">The son of David.</hi> His taking this title intimates, (1.) That he looked upon it as a great honour to be the son of so good a man, and valued himself very much upon it. (2.) That he also looked upon it as a great aggravation of his sin that he had such a father, who had given him a good education and put up many a good prayer for him; it cuts him to the heart to think that he should be a blemish and disgrace to the name and family of such a one as David. It aggravated the sin of Jehoiakim that he was the son of Josiah, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.15-Jer.22.17">Jer. xxii. 15-17</reference>. (3.) That his being the son of David encouraged him to repent and hope for mercy, for David had fallen into sin, by which he should have been warned not to sin, but was not; but David repented, and therein he took example from him and found mercy as he did. Yet this was not all; he was that son of David concerning whom God had said that though he would <hi type="italic">chasten his transgression with the rod,</hi> yet he would not <hi type="italic">break his covenant</hi> with him, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.34">Ps. lxxxix. 34</reference>. Christ, the great preacher, was the <hi type="italic">Son of David.</hi> <div eID="gen14834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14835" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">King of Jerusalem.</hi> This he mentions, (1.) As that which was a very great aggravation of his sin. He was a king. God had done much for him, in raising him to the throne, and yet he had so ill requited him; his dignity made the bad example and influence of his sin the more dangerous, and many would follow his pernicious ways; especially as he was king of Jerusalem, the holy city, where God's temple was, and of his own building too, where the priests, the Lord's ministers, were, and his prophets who had taught him better things. (2.) As that which might give some advantage to what he wrote, for <hi type="italic">where the word of a king is there is power.</hi> He thought it no disparagement to him, as a king, to be a preacher; but the people would regard him the more as a preacher because he was a king. If men of honour would lay out themselves to do good, what a great deal of good might they do! Solomon looked as great in the pulpit, preaching the vanity of the world, as in his throne of ivory, judging. <div eID="gen14835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14836" type="x-p"/> The Chaldee-paraphrase (which, in this book, makes very large additions to the text, or comments upon it, all along) gives this account of Solomon's writing this book, That by the spirit of prophecy he foresaw the revolt of the ten tribes from his son, and, in process of time, the destruction of Jerusalem and the house of the sanctuary, and the captivity of the people, in the foresight of which he said, <hi type="italic">Vanity of vanities, all is vanity;</hi> and to that he applies many passages in this book. <div eID="gen14836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14837" type="x-p"/> II. The general scope and design of the book. What is it that this royal preacher has to say? That which he aims at is, for the making of us truly religious, to take down our esteem of and expectation from the things of this world. In order to this, he shows, <div eID="gen14837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14838" type="x-p"/> 1. That they are <hi type="italic">all vanity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.2">v. 2</reference>. This is the proposition he lays down and undertakes to prove: <hi type="italic">Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.</hi> It was no new text; his father David had more than once spoken to the same purport. The truth itself here asserted is, that <hi type="italic">all is vanity,</hi> all besides God and considered as abstract from him, the <hi type="italic">all</hi> of this world, all worldly employments and enjoyments, the <hi type="italic">all</hi> that <hi type="italic">is in the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.2.16">1 John ii. 16</reference>), all that which is agreeable to our senses and to our fancies in this present state, which gains pleasure to ourselves or reputation with others. It is <hi type="italic">all vanity,</hi> not only in the abuse of it, when it is perverted by the sin of man, but even in the use of it. Man, considered with reference to these things, is vanity (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.5-Ps.39.6">Ps. xxxix. 5, 6</reference>), and, if there were not another life after this, were made in vain (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.47">Ps. lxxxix. 47</reference>); and those things, considered in reference to man (whatever they are in themselves), are <hi type="italic">vanity.</hi> They are impertinent to the soul, foreign, and add nothing to it; they do not answer the end, nor yield any true satisfaction; they are uncertain in their continuance, are fading, and perishing, and passing away, and will certainly deceive and disappoint those that put a confidence in them. Let us not therefore <hi type="italic">love vanity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">Ps. iv. 2</reference>), nor <hi type="italic">lift up our souls</hi> to it (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.4">Ps. xxiv. 4</reference>), for we shall but weary ourselves for it, <reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">Heb. ii. 13</reference>. It is expressed here very emphatically; not only, <hi type="italic">All is vain,</hi> but in the abstract, <hi type="italic">All is vanity;</hi> as if vanity were the <hi type="italic">proprium quarto modo—property in the fourth mode,</hi> of the things of this world, that which enters into the nature of them. The are not only <hi type="italic">vanity,</hi> but <hi type="italic">vanity of vanities,</hi> the vainest vanity, vanity in the highest degree, nothing but vanity, such a vanity as is the cause of a great deal of vanity. And this is redoubled, because the thing is certain and past dispute, it is <hi type="italic">vanity of vanities.</hi> This intimates that the wise man had his own heart fully convinced of and much affected with this truth, and that he was very desirous that others should be convinced of it and affected with it, as he was, but that he found the generality of men very loth to believe it and consider it (<reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job xxxiii. 14</reference>); it intimates likewise that we cannot comprehend and express the vanity of this world. But who is it that speaks thus slightly of the world? Is it one that will stand to what he says? Yes, he puts his name to it—<hi type="italic">saith the preacher.</hi> Is it one that was a competent judge? Yes, as much as ever any man was. Many speak contemptuously of the world because they are hermits, and know it not, or beggars, and have it not; but Solomon knew it. He had dived into nature's depths (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.33">1 Kings iv. 33</reference>), and he had it, more of it perhaps than ever any man had, his head filled with its notions and <hi type="italic">his belly</hi> with its <hi type="italic">hidden treasures</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.17.14">Ps. xvii. 14</reference>), and he passes this judgment on it. But did he speak as one having authority? Yes, not only that of a king, but that of a prophet, a preacher; he spoke in God's name, and was divinely inspired to say it. But did he not say it in his haste, or in a passion, upon occasion of some particular disappointment? No; he said it deliberately, said it and proved it, laid it down as a fundamental principle, on which he grounded the necessity of being religious. And, as some think, one main thing he designed was to show that the everlasting throne and kingdom which God had by Nathan promised to David and his seed must be of another world; for all things in this world are subject to vanity, and therefore have not in them sufficient to answer the extent of that promise. If Solomon find all to be vanity, then the kingdom of the Messiah must come, in which we shall inherit substance. <div eID="gen14838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14839" type="x-p"/> 2. That they are insufficient to make us happy. And for this he appeals to men's consciences: <hi type="italic">What profit has a man of all the pains he takes?</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.3">v. 3</reference>. Observe here, (1.) The business of this world described. It is <hi type="italic">labour;</hi> the word signifies both care and toil. It is work that wearies men. There is a constant fatigue in worldly business. It is <hi type="italic">labour under the sun;</hi> that is a phrase peculiar to this book, where we meet with it twenty-eight times. There is a world above the sun, a world which needs not the sun, for the glory of God is its light, where there is work without labour and with great profit, the work of angels; but he speaks of the work <hi type="italic">under the sun,</hi> the pains of which are great and the gains little. It is <hi type="italic">under the sun,</hi> under the influence of the sun, by its light and in its heat; as we have the benefit of the light of the day, so we have sometimes the burden and heat of the day (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.12">Matt. xx. 12</reference>), and therefore <hi type="italic">in the sweat of our face we eat bread.</hi> In the dark and cold grave the weary are at rest. (2.) The benefit of that business enquired into: <hi type="italic">What profit has a man of all that labour?</hi> Solomon says (<reference osisRef="Prov.14.23">Prov. xiv. 23</reference>), <hi type="italic">In all labour there is profit;</hi> and yet here he denies that there is any profit. As to our present condition in the world, it is true that by labour we get that which we call <hi type="italic">profit;</hi> we <hi type="italic">eat the labour of our hands;</hi> but as the wealth of the world is commonly called <hi type="italic">substance,</hi> and yet it is <hi type="italic">that which is not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.22.5">Prov. xxii. 5</reference>), so it is called <hi type="italic">profit,</hi> but the question is whether it be really so or no. And here he determines that it is not, that it is not a real benefit, that it is not a remaining benefit. In short, the wealth and pleasure of this world, if we had ever so much of them, are not sufficient to make us happy, nor will they be a portion for us. [1.] As to the body, and the life that now is, <hi type="italic">What profit has a man of all his labour? A man's life consists not in an abundance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.15">Luke xii. 15</reference>. As goods are increased care about them is increased, and <hi type="italic">those are increased that eat of them,</hi> and a little thing will embitter all the comfort of them; and then <hi type="italic">what profit has a man</hi> of all his labour? Early up, and never the nearer. [2.] As to the soul, and the life that is to come, we may much more truly say, <hi type="italic">What profit has a man of all his labour?</hi> All he gets by it will not supply the wants of the soul, nor satisfy its desires, will not atone for the sin of the soul, nor cure its diseases, nor contervail the loss of it; what profit will they be of to the soul in death, in judgment, or in the everlasting state? The fruit of our labour in heavenly things is <hi type="italic">meat that endures to eternal life,</hi> but the fruit of our labour for the world is only <hi type="italic">meat that perishes.</hi>
entries.021cf5de39483a8a8a4601ca9b862e5482028c46: <div eID="gen14839" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Vanity of the World.</title> <div sID="gen14840" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> <hi type="italic">One</hi> generation passeth away, and <hi type="italic">another</hi> generation cometh: but the earth abideth for ever. 5 The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose. <hi type="super">6</hi> The wind goeth toward the south, and turneth about unto the north; it whirleth about continually, and the wind returneth again according to his circuits. <hi type="super">7</hi> All the rivers run into the sea; yet the sea <hi type="italic">is</hi> not full; unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again. <hi type="super">8</hi> All things <hi type="italic">are</hi> full of labour; man cannot utter <hi type="italic">it:</hi> the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. <div eID="gen14840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14841" type="x-p"/> To prove the vanity of all things under the sun, and their insufficiency to make us happy, Solomon here shows, 1. That the time of our enjoyment of these things is very short, and only while we <hi type="italic">accomplish as a hireling his day.</hi> We continue in the world but for one generation, which is continually passing away to make room for another, and we are passing with it. Our worldly possessions we very lately had from others, and must very shortly leave to others, and therefore to us they are vanity; they can be no more substantial than that life which is the <hi type="italic">substratum</hi> of them, and that is but a <hi type="italic">vapour, which appears for a little while and then vanishes away.</hi> While the stream of mankind is continually flowing, how little enjoyment has one drop of that stream of the pleasant banks between which it glides! We may give God the glory of that constant succession of generations, in which the world has hitherto had its existence, and will have to the end of time, admitting his patience in continuing that sinful species and his power in continuing that dying species. We may be also quickened to do the work of our generation diligently, and serve it faithfully, because it will be over shortly; and, in concern for mankind in general, we should consult the welfare of succeeding generations; but as to our own happiness, let us not expect it within such narrow limits, but in an eternal rest and consistency. 2. That when we leave this world we leave the earth behind us, that <hi type="italic">abides for ever</hi> where it is, and therefore the things of the earth can stand us in no stead in the future state. It is well for mankind in general that the earth endures to the end of time, when it and all the works in it shall be burnt up; but what is that to particular persons, when they remove to the world of spirits? 3. That the condition of man is, in this respect, worse than that even of the inferior creatures: <hi type="italic">The earth abides for ever,</hi> but man abides upon the earth but a little while. The sun sets indeed every night, yet it rises again in the morning, as bright and fresh as ever; the winds, though they shift their point, yet in some point or other still they are; the waters that go to the sea above ground come from it again under ground. <hi type="italic">But man lies down and rises not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job xiv. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.14.12">12</reference>. 4. That all things in this world are movable and mutable, and subject to a continual toil and agitation, constant in nothing but inconstancy, still going, never resting; it was but once that the sun stood still; when it is risen it is hastening to set, and, when it is set, hastening to rise again (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.5">v. 5</reference>); the winds are ever and anon shifting (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">v. 6</reference>), and the waters in a continual circulation (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.7">v. 7</reference>), it would be of as bad consequence for them to stagnate as for the blood in the body to do so. And can we expect rest in a world where all things are thus full of labour (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">v. 8</reference>), on a sea that is always ebbing and flowing, and her waves continually working and rolling? 5. That though all things are still in motion, yet they are still where they were; The sun <hi type="italic">parts</hi> (as it is in the margin), but it is to the same place; the wind turns till it comes to the same place, and so the waters return to the place whence they came. Thus man, after all the pains he takes to find satisfaction and happiness in the creature, is but where he was, still as far to seek as ever. Man's mind is as restless in its pursuits as the sun, and wind, and rivers, but never satisfied, never contented; the more it has of the world the more it would have; and it would be no sooner filled with the streams of outward prosperity, the brooks of <hi type="italic">honey and butter</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.20.17">Job xx. 17</reference>), than the sea is with <hi type="italic">all the rivers that run into it;</hi> it is still as it was, <hi type="italic">a troubled sea that cannot rest.</hi> 6. That <hi type="italic">all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2 Pet. iii. 4</reference>. The earth is where it was; the sun, and winds, and rivers, keep the same course that ever they did; and therefore, if they have never yet been sufficient to make a happiness for man, they are never likely to be so, for they can but yield the same comfort that they have yielded. We must therefore look above the sun for satisfaction, and for a new world. 7. That this world is, at the best, a weary land: <hi type="italic">All is vanity,</hi> for all is <hi type="italic">full of labour.</hi> The whole creation is made subject to this vanity ever since man was sentenced to <hi type="italic">eat bread in the sweat of his brows.</hi> If we survey the whole creation, we shall see all busy; all have enough to do to mind their own business; none will be a portion or happiness for man; all labour to serve him, but none prove a <hi type="italic">help-meet</hi> for him. Man cannot express how full of labour all things are, can neither number the laborious nor measure the labours. 8. That our senses are unsatisfied, and the objects of them unsatisfying. He specifies those senses that perform their office with least toil, and are most capable of being pleased: <hi type="italic">The eye is not satisfied with seeing,</hi> but is weary of seeing always the same sight, and covets novelty and variety. <hi type="italic">The ear</hi> is fond, at first, of a pleasant song or tune, but soon nauseates it, and must have another; both are surfeited, but neither satiated, and what was most grateful becomes ungrateful. Curiosity is still inquisitive, because still unsatisfied, and the more it is humoured the more nice and peevish it grows, crying, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi>
entries.b3ad290a4ec42cdf25c2f70b9af39373e28b1d60: <div eID="gen14841" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Change without Novelty.</title> <div sID="gen14842" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> The thing that hath been, it <hi type="italic">is that</hi> which shall be; and that which is done <hi type="italic">is</hi> that which shall be done: and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no new <hi type="italic">thing</hi> under the sun. 10 Is there <hi type="italic">any</hi> thing whereof it may be said, See, this <hi type="italic">is</hi> new? it hath been already of old time, which was before us. <hi type="super">11</hi> <hi type="italic">There is</hi> no remembrance of former <hi type="italic">things;</hi> neither shall there be <hi type="italic">any</hi> remembrance of <hi type="italic">things</hi> that are to come with <hi type="italic">those</hi> that shall come after. <div eID="gen14842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14843" type="x-p"/> Two things we are apt to take a great deal of pleasure and satisfaction in, and value ourselves upon, with reference to our business and enjoyments in the world, as if they helped to save them from vanity. Solomon shows us our mistake in both. <div eID="gen14843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14844" type="x-p"/> 1. The novelty of the invention, that it is such as was never known before. How grateful is it to think that none ever made such advances in knowledge, and such discoveries by it, as we, that none ever made such improvements of an estate or trade, and had the art of enjoying the gains of it, as we have. Their contrivances and compositions are all despised and run down, and we boast of new fashions, new hypotheses, new methods, new expressions, which jostle out the old, and put them down. But this is all a mistake: <hi type="italic">The thing that</hi> is, and <hi type="italic">shall be, is</hi> the same with <hi type="italic">that which has been, and that which shall be done</hi> will be but the same with <hi type="italic">that which is done,</hi> for <hi type="italic">there is no new thing under the sun,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">v. 9</reference>. It is repeated (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.10">v. 10</reference>) by way of question, <hi type="italic">is there any thing</hi> of which <hi type="italic">it may be said,</hi> with wonder, <hi type="italic">See, this is new;</hi> there never was the like? It is an appeal to observing men, and a challenge to those that cry up modern learning above that of the ancients. Let them name any thing which they take to be new, and though perhaps we cannot make it to appear, for want of the records of former times, yet we have reason to conclude <hi type="italic">that it has been already of old time, which was before us.</hi> What is there in the kingdom of nature of which we may say, <hi type="italic">This is new? The works were finished from the foundation of the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.3">Heb. iv. 3</reference>); things which appear new to us, as they do to children, are not so in themselves. The heavens were <hi type="italic">of old;</hi> the earth abides for ever; the powers of nature and the links of natural causes are still the same that ever they were. In the kingdom of Providence, though the course and method of it have not such known and certain rules as that of nature, nor does it go always in the same track, yet, in the general, it is still the same thing over and over again. Men's hearts, and the corruptions of them, are still the same; their desires, and pursuits, and complaints, are still the same; and what God does in his dealings with men is according to the scripture, according to the manner, so that it is all repetition. What is surprising to us needs not be so, for there has been the like, the like strange advancements and disappointments, the like strange revolutions and sudden turns, sudden turns of affairs; the miseries of human life have always been much the same, and mankind tread a perpetual round, and, as the sun and wind, are but where they were. Now the design of this is, (1.) To show the folly of the children of men in affecting things that are new, in imagining that they have discovered such things, and in pleasing and priding themselves in them. We are apt to nauseate old things, and to grow weary of what we have been long used to, as Israel of the manna, and covet, with the Athenians, still to tell and hear of some new thing, and admire this and the other as new, whereas it is all what has been. Tatianus the Assyrian, showing the Grecians how all the arts which they valued themselves upon owed their original to those nations which they counted barbarous, thus reasons with them: "For shame, do not call those things <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">eureseis</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">inventions,</hi> which are but <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">mimeseis</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">imitations.</hi>" (2.) To take us off from expecting happiness or satisfaction in the creature. Why should we look for it there, where never any yet have found it? What reason have we to think that the world should be any kinder to us than it has been to those that have gone before us, since there is nothing in it that is new, and our predecessors have made as much of it as could be made? <hi type="italic">Your fathers did eat manna, and</hi> yet they <hi type="italic">are dead.</hi> See <reference osisRef="John.8.8-John.8.9">John viii. 8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.49">vi. 49</reference>. (3.) To quicken us to secure spiritual and eternal blessings. If we would be entertained with new things, we must acquaint ourselves with the things of God, get a new nature; then <hi type="italic">old things pass away, and all things become new,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.17">2 Cor. v. 17</reference>. The gospel puts <hi type="italic">a new song into our mouths.</hi> In heaven <hi type="italic">all is new</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.21.5">Rev. xxi. 5</reference>), all new at first, wholly unlike the present state of things, a new world indeed (<reference osisRef="Luke.20.35">Luke xx. 35</reference>), and all new to eternity, always fresh, always flourishing. This consideration should make us willing to die, That in this world there is nothing but the same over and over again, and we can expect nothing from it more or better than we have had. <div eID="gen14844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14845" type="x-p"/> 2. The memorableness of the achievement, that it is such as will be known and talked of hereafter. Many think they have found satisfaction enough in this, that their names shall be perpetuated, that posterity will celebrate the actions they have performed, the honours they have won, and the estates they have raised, that <hi type="italic">their houses shall continue for ever</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">Ps. xlix. 11</reference>); but herein they deceive themselves. How many <hi type="italic">former things</hi> and persons were there, which in their day looked very great and made a mighty figure, and yet <hi type="italic">there is no remembrance</hi> of them; they are buried in oblivion. Here and there one person or action that was remarkable met with a kind historian, and had the good hap to be recorded, when at the same time there were others, no less remarkable, that were dropped: and therefore we may conclude that <hi type="italic">neither shall there be any remembrance of things to come,</hi> but that which we hope to be remembered by will be either lost or slighted.
entries.910d752eeaba4eca07dbc7336f140f24598fdc7d: <div eID="gen14845" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Vanity of Human Wisdom.</title> <div sID="gen14846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">13</hi> And I gave my heart to seek and search out by wisdom concerning all <hi type="italic">things</hi> that are done under heaven: this sore travail hath God given to the sons of man to be exercised therewith. <hi type="super">14</hi> I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all <hi type="italic">is</hi> vanity and vexation of spirit. 15 <hi type="italic">That which is</hi> crooked cannot be made straight: and that which is wanting cannot be numbered. <hi type="super">16</hi> I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all <hi type="italic">they</hi> that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge. <hi type="super">17</hi> And I gave my heart to know wisdom, and to know madness and folly: I perceived that this also is vexation of spirit. <hi type="super">18</hi> For in much wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow. <div eID="gen14846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14847" type="x-p"/> Solomon, having asserted in general that <hi type="italic">all is vanity,</hi> and having given some general proofs of it, now takes the most effectual method to evince the truth of it, 1. By his own experience; he tried them all, and found them vanity. 2. By an induction of particulars; and here he begins with that which bids fairest of all to be the happiness of a reasonable creature, and that is knowledge and learning; if this be vanity, every thing else must needs be so. Now as to this, <div eID="gen14847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14848" type="x-p"/> I. Solomon tells us here what trial he had made of it, and that with such advantages that, if true satisfaction could have been found in it, he would have found it. 1. His high station gave him an opportunity of improving himself in all parts of learning, and particularly in politics and the conduct of human affairs, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12">v. 12</reference>. He that is <hi type="italic">the preacher</hi> of this doctrine <hi type="italic">was king over Israel,</hi> whom all their neighbours admired as <hi type="italic">a wise and understanding people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deut. iv. 6</reference>. He had his royal seat <hi type="italic">in Jerusalem,</hi> which then deserved, better than Athens ever did, to be called <hi type="italic">the eye of the world.</hi> The heart of a king is unsearchable; he has reaches of his own, and <hi type="italic">a divine sentence is often in his lips.</hi> It is his honour, it is his business, to search out every matter. Solomon's great wealth and honour put him into a capacity of making his court the centre of learning and the rendezvous of learned men, of furnishing himself with the best of books, and either conversing or corresponding with all the wise and knowing part of mankind then in being, who made application to him to learn of him, by which he could not but improve himself; for it is in knowledge as it is in trade, all the profit is by barter and exchange; if we have that to say which will instruct others, they will have that to say which will instruct us. Some observe how slightly Solomon speaks of his dignity and honour. He does not say, <hi type="italic">I the preacher am</hi> king, but I <hi type="italic">was king,</hi> no matter what I am. He speaks of it as a thing past, because worldly honours are transitory. 2. He applied himself to the improvement of these advantages, and the opportunities he had of getting wisdom, which, though ever so great, will not make a man wise unless he give his mind to it. Solomon <hi type="italic">gave his heart to seek and search out</hi> all things to be known <hi type="italic">by wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">v. 13</reference>. He made it his business to acquaint himself with <hi type="italic">all the things that are done under the sun,</hi> that are done by the providence of God or by the art and prudence of man. He set himself to get all the insight he could into philosophy and mathematics, into husbandry and trade, merchandise and mechanics, into the history of former ages and the present state of other kingdoms, their laws, customs, and policies, into men's different tempers, capacities, and projects, and the methods of managing them; he set himself not only to seek, but to search, to pry into, that which is most intricate, and which requires the closes application of mind and the most vigorous and constant prosecution. Though he was a prince, he made himself a drudge to learning, was not discouraged by its knots, nor took up short of its depths. And this he did, not merely to gratify his own genius, but to qualify himself for the service of God, and his generation, and to make an experiment how far the enlargement of the knowledge would go towards the settlement and repose of the mind. 3. He made a very great progress in his studies, wonderfully improved all the parts of learning, and carried his discoveries much further than any that had been before him. He did not condemn learning, as many do, because they cannot conquer it and will not be at the pains to make themselves masters of it; no, what he aimed at he compassed; he <hi type="italic">saw all the works that were done under the sun</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.14">v. 14</reference>), works of nature in the upper and lower world, all within this vortex (to use the modern gibberish) which has the sun for its centre, works of art, the product of men's wit, in a personal or social capacity. He had as much satisfaction in the success of his searches as ever any man had; he <hi type="italic">communed with his own heart</hi> concerning his attainments in knowledge, with as much pleasure as ever any rich merchant had in taking account of his stock. He could say, "<hi type="italic">Lo, I</hi> have magnified and increased <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> have not only gotten more of it myself, but have done more to propagate it and bring it into reputation, than any, <hi type="italic">than all that have been before me in Jerusalem.</hi>" Note, It becomes great men to be studious, and delight themselves most in intellectual pleasures. Where God gives great advantages of getting knowledge he expects improvements accordingly. It is happy with a people when their princes and noblemen study to excel others as much in wisdom and useful knowledge as they do in honour and estate; and they may do that service to the commonwealth of learning by applying themselves to the studies that are proper for them which meaner persons cannot do. Solomon must be acknowledged as competent judge of this matter, for he had not only got his head full of notions, but his <hi type="italic">heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge,</hi> of the power and benefit of knowledge, as well as the amusement and entertainment of it; what he knew he had digested, and knew how to make use of. <hi type="italic">Wisdom entered into his heart,</hi> and so became <hi type="italic">pleasant to his soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.2.10-Prov.2.11">Prov. ii. 10, 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.22.18">xxii. 18</reference>. 4. He applied his studies especially to that part of learning which is most serviceable to the conduct of human life, and consequently is the most valuable (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I gave my heart to know</hi> the rules and dictates of <hi type="italic">wisdom,</hi> and how I might obtain it; <hi type="italic">and to know madness and folly,</hi> how I might prevent and cure it, to know the snares and insinuations of it, that I might avoid them, and guard against them, and discover its fallacies." So industrious was Solomon to improve himself in knowledge that he gained instruction both by the wisdom of prudent men and by the madness of foolish men, by <hi type="italic">the field of the slothful,</hi> as well as of <hi type="italic">the diligent.</hi> <div eID="gen14848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14849" type="x-p"/> II. He tells us what was the result of this trial, to confirm what he had said, that <hi type="italic">all is vanity.</hi> <div eID="gen14849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14850" type="x-p"/> 1. He found that his searches after knowledge were very toilsome, and a weariness not only to the flesh, but to the mind (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">This sore travail,</hi> this difficulty that there is in searching after truth and finding it, <hi type="italic">God has given to the sons of men to be</hi> afflicted <hi type="italic">therewith,</hi> as a punishment for our first parents' coveting forbidden knowledge. As bread for the body, so that for the soul, must be got and eaten <hi type="italic">in the sweat of our face,</hi> whereas both would have been had with out labour if Adam had not sinned. <div eID="gen14850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14851" type="x-p"/> 2. He found that the more he saw of <hi type="italic">the works done under the sun</hi> the more he saw of their vanity; nay, and the sight often occasioned him <hi type="italic">vexation of spirit</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have seen all the works</hi> of a world full of business, have observed what the children of men are doing; <hi type="italic">and behold,</hi> whatever men think of their own works, I see <hi type="italic">all is vanity and vexation of spirit.</hi>" He had before pronounced all <hi type="italic">vanity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.2">v. 2</reference>), needless and unprofitable, and that which does us no good; here he adds, It is all <hi type="italic">vexation of spirit,</hi> troublesome and prejudicial, and that which does us hurt. It is <hi type="italic">feeding upon wind;</hi> so some read it, <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Hos. xii. 1</reference>. (1.) The works themselves which we see done are <hi type="italic">vanity and vexation</hi> to those that are employed in them. There is so much care in the contrivance of our worldly business, so much toil in the prosecution of it, and so much trouble in the disappointments we meet with in it, that we may well say, It is <hi type="italic">vexation of spirit.</hi> (2.) The sight of them is <hi type="italic">vanity and vexation of spirit</hi> to the wise observer of them. The more we see of the world the more we see to make us uneasy, and, with Heraclitus, to look upon all with weeping eyes. Solomon especially perceived that the knowledge of <hi type="italic">wisdom and folly</hi> was <hi type="italic">vexation of spirit,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">v. 17</reference>. It vexed him to see many that had wisdom not use it, and many that had folly not strive against it. It vexed him when he knew wisdom to see how far off it stood from the children of men, and, when he saw folly, to see how fast it was bound in their hearts. <div eID="gen14851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14852" type="x-p"/> 3. He found that when he had got some knowledge he could neither gain that satisfaction to himself nor do that good to others with it which he expected, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">v. 15</reference>. It would not avail, (1.) To redress the many grievances of human life: "After all, I find that <hi type="italic">that which is crooked</hi> will be crooked still and <hi type="italic">cannot be made straight.</hi>" Our knowledge is itself intricate and perplexed; we must go far about and fetch a great compass to come at it. Solomon thought to find out a nearer way to it, but he could not. The paths of learning are as much a labyrinth as ever they were. The minds and manners of men are crooked and perverse. Solomon thought, with his wisdom and power together, thoroughly to reform his kingdom, and make that straight which he found crooked; but he was disappointed. All the philosophy and politics in the world will not restore the corrupt nature of man to its primitive rectitude; we find the insufficiency of them both in others and in ourselves. Learning will not alter men's natural tempers, nor cure them of their sinful distempers; nor will it change the constitution of things in this world; a vale of tears it is and so it will be when all is done. (2.) To make up the many deficiencies in the comfort of human life: <hi type="italic">That which is wanting</hi> there <hi type="italic">cannot be numbered,</hi> or counted out to us from the treasures of human learning, but what <hi type="italic">is wanting</hi> will still be so. All our enjoyments here, when we have done our utmost to bring them to perfection, are still lame and defective, and it cannot be helped; as they are, so they are likely to be. <hi type="italic">That which is wanting</hi> in our knowledge is so much that it <hi type="italic">cannot be numbered.</hi> The more we know the more we see of our own ignorance. <hi type="italic">Who can understand his errors,</hi> his defects? <div eID="gen14852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14853" type="x-p"/> 4. Upon the whole, therefore, he concluded that great scholars do but make themselves great mourners; <hi type="italic">for in much wisdom is much grief,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.18">v. 18</reference>. There must be a great deal of pains taken to get it, and a great deal of care not to forget it; the more we know the more we see there is to be known, and consequently we perceive with greater clearness that our work is without end, and the more we see of our former mistakes and blunders, which occasions <hi type="italic">much grief.</hi> The more we see of men's different sentiments and opinions (and it is that which a great deal of our learning is conversant about) the more at a loss we are, it may be, which is in the right. Those <hi type="italic">that increase knowledge</hi> have so much the more quick and sensible perception of the calamities of this world, and for one discovery they make that is pleasing, perhaps, they make ten that are displeasing, and so they <hi type="italic">increase sorrow.</hi> Let us not therefore be driven off from the pursuit of any useful knowledge, but put on patience to break through the sorrow of it; but let us despair of finding true happiness in this knowledge, and expect it only in the knowledge of God and the careful discharge of our duty to him. <hi type="italic">He that increases</hi> in heavenly wisdom, and in an experimental acquaintance with the principles, powers, and pleasures of the spiritual and divine life, <hi type="italic">increases</hi> joy, such as will shortly be consummated in everlasting joy.  <chapter eID="Eccl.1"/> <div eID="gen14853" type="x-p"/>

entries.a4905e7b2fbcffc166788142ab4312c1edcbd1f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7978"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen12346" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew title is Koheleth, which the speaker in it applies to himself (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12">Ec 1:12</reference>), "I, Koheleth, was king over Israel." It means an Assembler or Convener of a meeting and a Preacher to such a meeting. The feminine form of the Hebrew noun, and its construction once (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.27">Ec 7:27</reference>) with a feminine verb, show that it not only signifies Solomon, the Preacher to assemblies (in which case it is construed with the verb or noun masculine), but also Divine Wisdom (feminine in Hebrew) speaking by the mouth of the inspired king. In six cases out of seven it is construed with the masculine. Solomon was endowed with inspired wisdom (1Ki 3:5-14; 6:<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.12">11, 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.1-1Kgs.9.9">9:1-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.9-1Cor.11.11">11:9-11</reference>), specially fitting him for the task. The Orientals delight in such meetings for grave discourse. Thus the Arabs formerly had an assembly yearly, at Ocadh, for hearing and reciting poems. Compare "Masters of assemblies" (see on <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.11">Ec 12:11</reference>, also <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.9">Ec 12:9</reference>). "The Preacher taught the people knowledge," probably viva voce ("orally"); <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.34">1Ki 4:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.2">10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.24">8, 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.1">2Ch 9:1</reference>, 7, 23, plainly refer to a somewhat public divan met for literary discussion. So "spake," thrice repeated (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.32">1Ki 4:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.33">33</reference>), refers not to written compositions, but to addresses spoken in assemblies convened for the purpose. The Holy Ghost, no doubt, signifies also by the term that Solomon's doctrine is intended for the "great congregation," the Church of all places and ages (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.25">Psa 22:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.2-Ps.49.4">49:2-4</reference>).<div eID="gen12346" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12345" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12347" type="x-p"/> Solomon was plainly the author (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12">Ec 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.16">16</reference>; 2:15; 12:9). That the Rabbins attribute it to Isaiah or Hezekiah is explicable by supposing that one or the other inserted it in the canon. The difference of its style, as compared with Proverbs and Song of Solomon, is due to the difference of subjects, and the different period of his life in which each was written; the Song, in the fervor of his first love to God; Proverbs, about the same time, or somewhat later; but Ecclesiastes in late old age, as the seal and testimony of repentance of his apostasy in the intervening period: <reference osisRef="Ps.89.30">Psa 89:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.33">33</reference> proves his penitence. The substitution of the title Koheleth for Solomon (that is, peace), may imply that, having troubled Israel, meantime he forfeited his name of peace (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.14">1Ki 11:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.23">23</reference>); but now, having repented, he wishes to be henceforth a Preacher of righteousness. The alleged foreign expressions in the Hebrew may have been easily imported, through the great intercourse there was with other nations during his long reign. Moreover, supposed Chaldaisms may be fragments preserved from the common tongue of which Hebrew, Syriac, Chaldee, and Arabic were offshoots.<div eID="gen12347" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12348" type="x-p"/> The Scope of Ecclesiastes is to show the vanity of all mere human pursuits, when made the chief end, as contrasted with the real blessedness of true wisdom, that is, religion. The immortality of the soul is dwelt on incidentally, as subsidiary to the main scope. Moses' law took this truth for granted but drew its sanctions of rewards and punishments in accordance with the theocracy, which was under a special providence of God as the temporal King of Israel, from the present life, rather than the future. But after Israel chose an earthly king, God withdrew, in part, His extraordinary providence, so that under Solomon, temporal rewards did not invariably follow virtue, and punishments vice (compare <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.16">Ec 2:16</reference>; 3:19; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.1">4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.8">5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.15">7:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.14">8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">9:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.11">11</reference>). Hence the need arises to show that these anomalies will be rectified hereafter, and this is the grand "conclusion," therefore, of the "whole" book, that, seeing there is a coming judgment, and seeing that present goods do not satisfy the soul, "man's whole duty is to fear God and keep his commandments" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">Ec 12:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.14">14</reference>), and meanwhile, to use, in joyful and serene sobriety, and not abuse, the present life (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen12348" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12349" type="x-p"/> It is objected that sensual epicurism seems to be inculcated (<reference osisRef="Eccl.3.12">Ec 3:12</reference>, 13, 22, &c.); but it is a contented, thankful enjoyment of God's present gifts that is taught, as opposed to a murmuring, anxious, avaricious spirit, as is proved by <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">Ec 5:18</reference>, compare with <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11-Eccl.5.15">Ec 5:11-15</reference>, not making them the chief end of life; not the joy of levity and folly; a misunderstanding which he guards against in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.2-Eccl.6.11">Ec 7:2-6; 11</reference>:9; 12:1. Again, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.16">Ec 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2-Eccl.9.10">9:2-10</reference>, might seem to teach fatalism and skepticism. But these are words put in the mouth of an objector; or rather, they were the language of Solomon himself during his apostasy, finding an echo in the heart of every sensualist, who wishes to be an unbeliever, and, who, therefore, sees difficulties enough in the world around wherewith to prop up his wilful unbelief. The answer is given (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.17">Ec 7:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.18">18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.11">9:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.12">12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.13">12:13</reference>). Even if these passages be taken as words of Solomon, they are to be understood as forbidding a self-made "righteousness," which tries to constrain God to grant salvation to imaginary good works and external strictness with which it wearies itself; also, that speculation which tries to fathom all God's inscrutable counsels (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.17">Ec 8:17</reference>), and that carefulness about the future forbidden in <reference osisRef="Matt.6.25">Mt 6:25</reference>.<div eID="gen12349" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12350" type="x-p"/> The Chief Good is that the possession of that which makes us happy, is to be sought as the end, for its own sake; whereas, all other things are but means towards it. Philosophers, who made it the great subject of inquiry, restricted it to the present life, treating the eternal as unreal, and only useful to awe the multitude with. But Solomon shows the vanity of all human things (so-called philosophy included) to satisfy the soul, and that heavenly wisdom alone is the chief good. He had taught so when young (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.20">Pr 1:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.1">8:1</reference>); so also; in Song of Solomon, he had spiritualized the subject in an allegory; and now, after having long personally tried the manifold ways in which the worldly seek to reach happiness, he gives the fruit of his experience in old age.<div eID="gen12350" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12351" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">It is divided into two parts--</hi>Ec 1:<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.10">1-6:10</reference> showing the vanity of earthly things; Ec 6:10-12:14, the excellence of heavenly wisdom. Deviations from strict logical methods occur in these divisions, but in the main they are observed. The deviations make it the less stiff and artificial, and the more suited to all capacities. It is in poetry; the hemistichal division is mostly observed, but occasionally not so. The choice of epithets, imagery, inverted order of words, ellipses, parallelism, or, in its absence, similarity of diction, mark versification.<div eID="gen12351" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Eccl.1.1-Eccl.1.18">Ec 1:1-18</reference>. Introduction.</title> <div sID="gen12352" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7978"/><hi type="bold">1. the Preacher--</hi>and Convener of assemblies for the purpose. See my Preface. Koheleth in Hebrew, a symbolical name for Solomon, and of Heavenly Wisdom speaking through and identified with him. <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12">Ec 1:12</reference> shows that "king of Jerusalem" is in apposition, not with "David," but "Preacher."<div eID="gen12352" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12353" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Jerusalem--</hi>rather, "in Jerusalem," for it was merely his metropolis, not his whole kingdom. <div eID="gen12353" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2713a31078df7ddd47bc2fd11eb20c862e05aa2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7979"/><div sID="gen12354" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7979"/>2. The theme proposed of the first part of his discourse.<div eID="gen12354" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12355" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Vanity of vanities--</hi>Hebraism for the most utter vanity. So "holy of holies" (<reference osisRef="Exod.26.33">Ex 26:33</reference>); "servant of servants" (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">Ge 9:25</reference>). The repetition increases the force.<div eID="gen12355" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12356" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>Hebrew, "the all"; all without exception, namely, earthly things.<div eID="gen12356" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12357" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vanity--</hi>not in themselves, for God maketh nothing in vain (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4">1Ti 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.5">5</reference>), but vain when put in the place of God and made the end, instead of the means (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.5">Psa 39:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.9">62:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Mt 6:33</reference>); vain, also, because of the "vanity" to which they are "subjected" by the fall (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.20">Ro 8:20</reference>). <div eID="gen12357" type="x-p"/>
entries.91673d47ce9b868dfd92b63ba2afec7dfc5aa86d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7980"/><div sID="gen12358" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7980"/><hi type="bold">3. What profit ... labour--</hi>that is, "What profit" as to the chief good (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Mt 16:26</reference>). Labor is profitable in its proper place (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.15">Ge 2:15</reference>; 3:19; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.23">Pr 14:23</reference>).<div eID="gen12358" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12359" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">under the sun--</hi>that is, in this life, as opposed to the future world. The phrase often recurs, but only in Ecclesiastes. <div eID="gen12359" type="x-p"/>
entries.d53a46b7b992bd98d92cf305a8499433e0b20147: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7981"/><div sID="gen12360" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7981"/><hi type="bold">4. earth ... for ever--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.104.5">Psa 104:5</reference>). While the earth remains the same, the generations of men are ever changing; what lasting profit, then, can there be from the toils of one whose sojourn on earth, as an individual, is so brief? The "for ever" is comparative, not absolute (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference>). <div eID="gen12360" type="x-p"/>
entries.e5358b0985e1756372082033c4e748a10bbb8c09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7982"/><div sID="gen12361" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7982"/>5. (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.5">Psa 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.19.6">6</reference>). "Panting" as the Hebrew for "hasteth"; metaphor, from a runner (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.5">Psa 19:5</reference>, "a strong man") in a "race." It applies rather to the rising sun, which seems laboriously to mount up to the meridian, than to the setting sun; the accents too favor Maurer, "And (that too, returning) to his place, where panting he riseth." <div eID="gen12361" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e21b45a9aa76ed10ecb6263c380f65576ad5113: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7983"/><div sID="gen12362" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7983"/><hi type="bold">6. according to his circuits--</hi>that is, it returns afresh to its former circuits, however many be its previous veerings about. The north and south winds are the two prevailing winds in Palestine and Egypt. <div eID="gen12362" type="x-p"/>
entries.0d9f275e3a843b600d3544752cac871bce3226ab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7984"/><div sID="gen12363" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7984"/>7. By subterraneous cavities, and by evaporation forming rain clouds, the fountains and rivers are supplied from the sea, into which they then flow back. The connection is: Individual men are continually changing, while the succession of the race continues; just as the sun, wind, and rivers are ever shifting about, while the cycle in which they move is invariable; they return to the point whence they set out. Hence is man, as in these objects of nature which are his analogue, with all the seeming changes "there is no new thing" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ec 1:9</reference>). <div eID="gen12363" type="x-p"/>
entries.7ac824d8163a1a06bfe4de2394c08ee63b07d2b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7985"/><div sID="gen12364" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7985"/>8. Maurer translates, "All words are wearied out," that is, are inadequate, as also, "man cannot express" all the things in the world which undergo this ceaseless, changeless cycle of vicissitudes: "The eye is not satisfied with seeing them," &c. But it is plainly a return to the idea (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.3">Ec 1:3</reference>) as to man's "labor," which is only wearisome and profitless; "no new" good can accrue from it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ec 1:9</reference>); for as the sun, &c., so man's laborious works move in a changeless cycle. The eye and ear are two of the taskmasters for which man toils. But these are never "satisfied" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Ec 6:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pr 27:20</reference>). Nor can they be so hereafter, for there will be nothing "new." Not so the chief good, Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="John.4.13">Joh 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.4.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.5">Re 21:5</reference>). <div eID="gen12364" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed24ef4676ff4c5c983c2a8d69f9c2ec12cca887: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7986"/><div sID="gen12365" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7986"/>9. Rather, "no new thing at all"; as in <reference osisRef="Num.11.6">Nu 11:6</reference>. This is not meant in a general sense; but there is no new source of happiness (the subject in question) which can be devised; the same round of petty pleasures, cares, business, study, wars, &c., being repeated over and over again [Holden]. <div eID="gen12365" type="x-p"/>
entries.954f90dff162a9ede6e79c19334cbbb1e4c9d37c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7987"/><div sID="gen12366" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7987"/><hi type="bold">10. old time--</hi>Hebrew, "ages."<div eID="gen12366" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12367" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which was--</hi>The Hebrew plural cannot be joined to the verb singular. Therefore translate: "It hath been in the ages before; certainly it hath been before us" [Holden]. Or, as Maurer: "That which has been (done) before us (in our presence, <reference osisRef="1Chr.16.33">1Ch 16:33</reference>), has been (done) already in the old times." <div eID="gen12367" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5ea95d71e98a8eaedb67526a6be77c0bf744485: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7988"/><div sID="gen12368" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7988"/>11. The reason why some things are thought "new," which are not really so, is the imperfect record that exists of preceding ages among their successors.<div eID="gen12368" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12369" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">those that ... come after--</hi>that is, those that live still later than the "things, rather the persons or generations, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">Ec 1:4</reference>, with which this verse is connected, the six intermediate verses being merely illustrations of <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">Ec 1:4</reference> [Weiss], that are to come" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.16">Ec 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.5">9:5</reference>). <div eID="gen12369" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d625c0f4a7c2c6d4c1c6d750ec3e4810724cf5d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7989"/><div sID="gen12370" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7989"/>12. Resumption of <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.1">Ec 1:1</reference>, the intermediate verses being the introductory statement of his thesis. Therefore, "the Preacher" (Koheleth) is repeated.<div eID="gen12370" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12371" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was king--</hi>instead of "am," because he is about to give the results of his past experience during his long reign.<div eID="gen12371" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12372" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in Jerusalem--</hi>specified, as opposed to David, who reigned both in Hebron and Jerusalem; whereas Solomon reigned only in Jerusalem. "King of Israel in Jerusalem," implies that he reigned over Israel and Judah combined; whereas David, at Hebron, reigned only over Judah, and not, until he was settled in Jerusalem, over both Israel and Judah. <div eID="gen12372" type="x-p"/>
entries.227ea852d505f5551c571583837379e9c922d7df: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7990"/><div sID="gen12373" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7990"/><hi type="bold">13. this sore travail--</hi>namely, that of "searching out all things done under heaven." Not human wisdom in general, which comes afterwards (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.12">Ec 2:12</reference>, &c.), but laborious enquiries into, and speculations about, the works of men; for example, political science. As man is doomed to get his bread, so his knowledge, by the sweat of his brow (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.19">Ge 3:19</reference>) [Gill].<div eID="gen12373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12374" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exercised--</hi>that is, disciplined; literally, "that they may thereby chastise, or humble themselves." <div eID="gen12374" type="x-p"/>
entries.64378bff9bc88c8f8c7889eb294620a112261e86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7991"/><div sID="gen12375" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7991"/>14. The reason is here given why investigation into man's "works" is only "sore travail" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ec 1:13</reference>); namely, because all man's ways are vain (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.18">Ec 1:18</reference>) and cannot be mended (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">Ec 1:15</reference>).<div eID="gen12375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12376" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vexation of--</hi>"a preying upon"<div eID="gen12376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12377" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Spirit--</hi>Maurer translates; "the pursuit of wind," as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.16">Ec 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.1">Ho 12:1</reference>, "Ephraim feedeth on wind." But old versions support the English Version. <div eID="gen12377" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d1a0604455615d950ad074728967ea776e6730a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7992"/><div sID="gen12378" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7992"/>15. Investigation (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ec 1:13</reference>) into human ways is vain labor, for they are hopelessly "crooked" and "cannot be made straight" by it (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13">Ec 7:13</reference>). God, the chief good, alone can do this (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.4">Is 40:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.2">45:2</reference>).<div eID="gen12378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12379" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wanting--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.5.27">Da 5:27</reference>).<div eID="gen12379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12380" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">numbered--</hi>so as to make a complete number; so equivalent to "supplied" [Maurer]. Or, rather, man's state is utterly wanting; and that which is wholly defective cannot be numbered or calculated. The investigator thinks he can draw up, in accurate numbers, statistics of man's wants; but these, including the defects in the investigator's labor, are not partial, but total. <div eID="gen12380" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4aa44481bf0b0cd96471ec88cb0123c2a3aa32e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7993"/><div sID="gen12381" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7993"/><hi type="bold">16. communed with ... heart--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.24.45">Ge 24:45</reference>).<div eID="gen12381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12382" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come to great estate--</hi>Rather, "I have magnified and gotten" (literally, "added," increased), &c.<div eID="gen12382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12383" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all ... before me in Jerusalem--</hi>namely, the priests, judges, and two kings that preceded Solomon. His wisdom exceeded that of all before Jesus Christ, the antitypical Koheleth, or "Gatherer of men," (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.34">Lu 13:34</reference>), and "Wisdom" incarnate (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.19">Mt 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.12.42">12:42</reference>).<div eID="gen12383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12384" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had ... experience--</hi>literally, "had seen" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.31">Jr 2:31</reference>). Contrast with this glorying in worldly wisdom (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.23">Jr 9:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.9.24">24</reference>). <div eID="gen12384" type="x-p"/>
entries.a63d9af598d10b9f9b2ea2fda2f1122e56372f26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7994"/><div sID="gen12385" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7994"/><hi type="bold">17. wisdom ... madness--</hi>that is, their effects, the works of human wisdom and folly respectively. "Madness," literally, "vaunting extravagance"; <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.12">Ec 2:12</reference>; 7:25, &c., support English Version rather than Dathe, "splendid matters." "Folly" is read by English Version with some manuscripts, instead of the present Hebrew text, "prudence." If Hebrew be retained, understand "prudence," falsely so called (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>), "craft" (<reference osisRef="Dan.8.25">Da 8:25</reference>). <div eID="gen12385" type="x-p"/>
entries.ce62b1afff17e0bec626cb33c4e33c1e3ccf3cdd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7995"/><div sID="gen12386" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7995"/><hi type="bold">18. wisdom ... knowledge--</hi>not in general, for wisdom, &c., are most excellent in their place; but speculative knowledge of man's ways (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ec 1:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>), which, the farther it goes, gives one the more pain to find how "crooked" and "wanting" they are (<reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">Ec 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.12">12:12</reference>). <chapter eID="Eccl.1"/>

entries.3efd90df0663967fdafd975b7e425bf5f9ade380: <div eID="gen25121" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Book of Ecclesiastes</title> <div sID="gen25122" type="x-p"/> The book, entitled Koheleth, or Ecclesiastes, has ever been received, both by the Jewish and Christian Church, as written under the inspiration of the Almighty; and was held to be properly a part of the sacred canon. But while this has been almost universally granted, there has been but little unanimity among learned men and critics as to its author.
