And also women who were a misfortune to their husbands or lovers there have always been, so that in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ecc 7:26</reference> one does not need to think of that Agathoclea who ruled over Ptolemy Philopator, and even had in her hands the power of life and death. <div eID="gen12184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12185" type="x-p"/> Passages such as <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Ecc 7:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ecc 7:26</reference> afford no help in reference to the chronology. On the other hand, the author in <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.13-Eccl.9.16">Ecc 9:13-16</reference> relates, to all appearance, what he himself experienced. But the little city is certainly not the fortified town of Dora, on the sea-coast to the west of Carmel, which was besieged by Antiochus the Great (Polybius, v. 66) in the year 218, as at a later period, in the year 138, it was by Antiochus VII, Sidetes (Joseph. <hi type="italic">Bell</hi>. i. 2. 2); for this Dora was not then saved by a poor wise man within it, - of whom Polybius knows nothing, - but “by the strength of the place, and the help of those with Nicholaus.” A definite historical event is also certainly found in <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13">Ecc 4:13</reference>-16. Hitzig sees in the old foolish king the spiritually contracted, but so much the more covetous, high priest Onias, under Ptolemy Euergetes; and in the poor but wise youth, Joseph (the son of Tobias), who robbed Onias of his place in the state, and raised himself to the office of general farmer of taxes. But here nothing agrees but that Onias was old and foolish, and that Joseph was then a young wise man (Joseph. <hi type="italic">Antt.</hi> xii. 4. 2); of the poverty of the latter nothing is heard-he was the nephew of Onias. And besides, he did not come out of the house “of prisoners” (הסוּרים); this word is pointed by Hitzig so as to mean, out of the house “of fugitives” (הסּוּרים), perhaps, as he supposes, an allusion to the district Φιχόλα, which the author thus interprets as if it were derived from φεύγειν. Historical investigation has here degenerated into the boldest subjectivism. The Heb. tongue has never called “fugitives” הסורים; and to whom could the Heb. word פיקולה (cf. <hi type="italic">Berachoth</hi> 28b) suggest - as Φύγελα did to Pliny and Mela - the Greek φεύγειν! <div eID="gen12185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12186" type="x-p"/> We have thus, in determining the time of the authorship of this book, to confine ourselves to the period subsequent to the Diadochs. It may be regarded as beyond a doubt that it was written under the Persian domination. Kleinert (<hi type="italic">Der Prediger Salomo</hi>, 1864) is in general right in saying that the political condition of the people which the book presupposes, is that in which they are placed under Satraps; the unrighteous judgment, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ecc 3:16</reference>; and the despotic oppression, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ecc 4:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.9">Ecc 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Ecc 5:7</reference>; the riotous court-life, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16-Eccl.10.19">Ecc 10:16-19</reference>; the raising of mean men to the highest places of honour, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.5-Eccl.10.7">Ecc 10:5-7</reference>; the inexorable severity of the law of war-service, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.8">Ecc 8:8</reference>;<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Herod. iv. 84, vii. 38f.</note> the prudence required by the organized system of espionage<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Duncker’s <hi type="italic">Gesch. des Alterthums</hi>, Bd. 2 (1867), p. 894.</note> existing at such a time, - all these things were characteristic of this period. But if the Book of Koheleth is not at all older than Malachi, then it was written somewhere within the last century of the Persian kingdom, between Artaxerxes I, Longimanus (464-424), and Darius Codomannus (335-332): the better days for the Jewish people, of the Persian supremacy under the first five Achaemenides, were past (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Ecc 7:10</reference>). <div eID="gen12186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12187" type="x-p"/> Indeed, in <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">Ecc 6:3</reference> there appear to be reminiscences of Artaxerxes II, Mnemon (died about 360), who was 94 years old, and, according to Justin (x. 1), had 115 sons, and of Artaxerxes III, Ochus his successor, who was poisoned by the chief eunuch Bagoas, who, according to Aelian, <hi type="italic">Var. Hist</hi>. vi. 8, threw his (Ochus') body to the cats, and caused sword-handles to be made from his bones. The book altogether contains many examples to which concrete instances in the Persian history correspond, from which they might be abstracted, in which strict harmony on all sides with historical fact is not to be required, since it did not concern the author. The event recorded Ecc 4:13. refers to Cyrus rising to the supremacy of world-ruler (after dispossessing the old Median King Astyages), who left<note placement="foot">According to Nicolaus of Damascus (Müller’s <hi type="italic">Fragm. hist. Graec</hi>. III 398), Cyrus was the child of poor parents; by “prison-house” (<reference osisRef="Eccl.4.14">Ecc 4:14</reference>), reference is made to his confinement in Persia, where access to him was prevented by guards (Herod. i. 123). Justin, i. 5: “A letter could not be openly brought to him, since the guards appointed by the king kept possession of all approaches to him.”</note> nothing but misery to posterity. Such a rich man as is described in <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">Ecc 6:2</reference>, who had to leave all his treasures to a stranger, was Croesus, to whom Solon, as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.7.8">Ecc 7:8</reference></hi> (cf. Herod. i. 32, 86), said that no one ought to be praised before his end. A case analogous at least to <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.14-Eccl.9.16">Ecc 9:14-16</reference>, was the deliverance of Athens by the counsel of Themistocles (Justin, ii. 12), who finally, driven from Athens, was compelled to seek the protection of the Persian king, and ended his life in despair.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Spiegel’s <hi type="italic">Erânische Alterthumskunde</hi>, II pp. 409, 413. Bernstein suggests the deliverance of Potidea (Herod. viii. 128) or Tripolis (Diodor. xvi. 41); but neither of these cities owed its deliverance to the counsel of a wise man. Burger (<hi type="italic">Comm. in Ecclesiasten</hi>, 1864) thinks, with greater probability, of Themistocles, who was celebrated among the Persians (Thucyd. i. 138), which Ewald also finds most suitable, provided the author had a definite fact before his eye.</note> <div eID="gen12187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12188" type="x-p"/> If we were not confined, for the history of the Persian kingdom and its provinces, from Artaxerxes I to the appearance of Alexander of Macedon, to only a few and scanty sources of information (we know no Jewish events of this period, except the desecration of the temple by Bagoses, described by Josephus, <hi type="italic">Antt.</hi> xi. 7), we might probably be better able to understand many of the historical references of the Book of Koheleth. We should then be able to say to whom the author refers by the expression, “Woe to thy land when thy king is a child,” <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.16">Ecc 10:16</reference>; for Artaxerxes I, who, although only as yet a boy at the time of the murder of his father Xerxes (Justin, iii. 1), soon thereafter appeared manly enough, cannot be thought of. We should then, perhaps, be also in possession of the historical key to <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.10">Ecc 8:10</reference>; for with the reference to the deportation of many thousands of Jewish prisoners (Josephus, <hi type="italic">c. Ap.</hi> i. 22) - which, according to Syncellus and Orosius, must have occurred under Artaxerxes III, Ochus - the interpretation of that passage does not accord.<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Bernstein’s <hi type="italic">Quaestiones Kohelethanae</hi>, p. 66.</note> <div eID="gen12188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12189" type="x-p"/> We should then also, perhaps, know to what political arrangement the author points when he says, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.19">Ecc 7:19</reference>, that wisdom is a stronger protection to a city than “ten mighty men;” Grätz refers this to the <hi type="italic">decuriones</hi> of the Roman municipal cities and colonies; but probably it refers to the dynasties<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., Duncker’s <hi type="italic">Gesch. des Alterthums</hi>, II p. 910.</note> (cf. Assyr. salat, governor) placed by the Persian kings over the cities of conquered countries. And generally, the oppressed spirit pervading the book would be so much clearer if we knew more of the sacrifices which the Jewish people in the later time of the Persians had to make, than merely that the Phoenicians, at the same time with “The Syrians in Palestine,” had to contribute (Herod. vii. 87) to Xerxes for his Grecian expedition three hundred triremes; and also that the people who “dwelt in the Solymean mountains” had to render him assistance in his expedition against Greece (Joseph. <hi type="italic">c. Ap.</hi> i. 22). <div eID="gen12189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12190" type="x-p"/> The author was without doubt a Palestinian. In Eccl 4:17 he speaks of himself as dwelling where the temple was, and also in the holy city, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.10">Ecc 8:10</reference>; he lived, if not actually in it, at least in its near neighbourhood, <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">Ecc 10:15</reference>; although, as Kleinert remarks, he appears, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.1">Ecc 11:1</reference>, to make use of a similitude taken from the corn trade of a seaport town. From <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.8">Ecc 4:8</reference> the supposition is natural that he was alone in the land, without children or brothers or sisters; but from the contents and spirit of the whole book, it appears more certain that, like his Koheleth, he was advanced in years, and had behind him a long checkered life. The symptoms of approaching death presenting themselves in old age, which he describes to the young, Ecc 12:2., he probably borrowed from his own experience. The whole book bears the marks of age, - a production of the Old Covenant which was stricken in age, and fading away. <div eID="gen12190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12191" type="x-p"/> The literature, down to 1860, of commentaries and monographs on the Book of Koheleth is very fully set forth in the English Commentary of Ginsburg, and from that time to 1867, in Zöckler’s Commentary, which forms a part of Lange’s <hi type="italic">Bibelwerk</hi>. Keil’s <hi type="italic">Einleitung</hi>, 3rd ed. 1873, contains a supplement to these, among which, however, the <hi type="italic">Bonner Theolog. Literaturblatt</hi>, 1874, Nr. 7, misses Pusey’s and Reusch’s (cf. the <hi type="italic">Tübingen Theol. Quartalschrift</hi>, 1860, pp. 430-469). It is not possible for any man to compass this literature. Aedner’s <hi type="italic">Catalogue of the Hebrew books in the Library of the British Museum</hi>, 1867, contains a number of Jewish commentaries omitted by Ginsburg and Zöckler, but far from all. For example, the Commentary of Ahron B. Josef (for the first time printed at Eupatoria, 1834) now lies before me, with those of Moses Frankel (Dessau, 1809), and of Samuel David Luzzatto, in the journal, <hi type="italic">Ozar Nechmad</hi> 1864. Regarding the literature of English interpretation, see the American translation, by Tayler Lewis (1870), of Zöckler’s Commentary. The catalogue there also is incomplete, for in 1873 a Commentary by Thomas Pelham Dale appeared; and a Monograph on <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.1-Eccl.12.14">Ecc 12:1-14</reference>, under the title of <hi type="italic">The Dirge of Coheleth</hi>, by the Orientalist C. Taylor, appeared in 1874. The fourth volume of the <hi type="italic">Speaker’s Commentary</hi> contains a Commentary on the Song by Kingsbury, and on Ecclesiastes by W. T. Bullock, who strenuously maintains its Solomonic authorship. The opinion that the book represents the conflict of two voices, the voice of true wisdom and that of pretended wisdom, has lately found advocates not only in a Hebrew Commentary by Ephraim Hirsch (Warsaw, 1871), but also in the article “Koheleth” by Schenkel in his <hi type="italic">Bibellexikon</hi> (vol. III, 1871). For the history and refutation of this attempt to represent the book in the form of a dialogue, we might refer to Zöckler’s Introd. to his Commentary. <div eID="gen12191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12192" type="x-p"/> The old translations have been referred to at length by Ginsburg. Frederick Field, in his <hi type="italic">Hexapla</hi> (Poet. vol. 1867), has collected together the fragments of the Greek translations. Ge. Janichs, in his <hi type="italic">Animadversiones criticae</hi> (Breslau, 1871), has examined the Peshito of Koheleth and Ruth; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., with reference thereto, Nöldeke’s <hi type="italic">Anzeige</hi> in the <hi type="italic">Liter. Centralblatt</hi> 1871, Nr. 49, and cf. Middeldorpf’s <hi type="italic">Symbolae exegetico-criticae ad librum Ecclesiastis</hi>, 1811. The text of the <hi type="italic">Graecus Venetus</hi> lies before us now in a more accurate form than that by Villoison (1784), in Gebhardt’s careful edition of certain Venetian manuscripts (Leipzig, Brockhaus 1874), containing this translation of the O.T. books. <div eID="gen12192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12193" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.1">Ecc 1:1</reference> <div eID="gen12193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12194" type="x-p"/> The title, <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.1">Ecc 1:1</reference>, <hi type="italic">The words of Koheleth, son of David, king in Jerusalem</hi>, has been already explained in the Introduction. The verse, which does not admit of being properly halved, is rightly divided by “son of David” by the accent <hi type="italic">Zakef</hi>; for the apposition, “king in Jerusalem,” does not belong to “David,” but to “Koheleth.” In several similar cases, such as <reference osisRef="Ezek.1.3">Eze 1:3</reference>, the accentuation leaves the designation of the oppositional genitive undefined; in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Gen.10.21">Gen 10:21</reference></hi> it proceeds on an erroneous supposition; it is rightly defined in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Amo 1:1</reference></hi>, for example, as in the passage before us. That “king” is without the article, is explained from this, that it is determined by “in Jerusalem,” as elsewhere by “of Israel” (“Judah”). The expression (cf. 2Ki 14:23) is singular.
entries.56a65bfec9f1595aac7996494efff9891ec347ab: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.2">Ecc 1:2</reference> <div eID="gen12194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12195" type="x-p"/> The book begins artistically with an opening section of the nature of a preamble. The ground-tone of the whole book at once sounds in <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.2">Ecc 1:2</reference>, which commences this section, “O vanity of vanities, saith Koheleth, O vanity of vanities! All is vain.” As at <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>) it is a question whether by “saith” is meant a future or a present utterance of God, so here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.8">Ecc 12:8</reference> whether “saith” designates the expression of Koheleth as belonging to history or as presently given forth. The language admits both interpretations, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, “saith,” with God as the subject, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2Sa 23:3</reference>, is meant historically, and in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">Isa 49:5</reference> of the present time. We understand “saith” here, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.36.4">Isa 36:4</reference>, “Thus saith ... the king of Assyria,” of something said now, not of something said previously, since it is those presently living to whom the Solomon <hi type="italic">redivivus</hi>, and through him the author of this book, preaches the vanity of all earthly things. The old translators take “vanity of vanities” in the nominative, as if it were the predicate; but the repetition of the expression shows that it is an exclamation = <hi type="italic">O vanitatem vanitatum</hi>. The abbreviated connecting form of הבל is here not punctuated הבל, after the form חדר (חדר) and the like, but הבל, after the manner of the Aram. ground-form עבד; cf. Ewald, §32 <hi type="italic">b</hi>. Jerome read differently: <hi type="italic">In Hebraeo pro vanitate vanitatum ABAL ABALIM scriptum est, quod exceptis</hi> lxx <hi type="italic">interpretibus omnes similiter transtulerunt</hi> ἀτμὸς ἀτμἰδων <hi type="italic">sive</hi> ἀτμῶν. Hěvěl primarily signifies a breath, and still bears this meaning in post-bibl. Heb., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <hi type="italic">Schabbath</hi> 119 <hi type="italic">b</hi>: “The world exists merely for the sake of the breath of school-children” (who are the hope of the future). Breath, as the contrast of that which is firm and enduring, is the figure of that which has no support, no continuance. Regarding the superlative expression, “Vanity of vanities,” <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the Sol 1:1. “Vanity of vanities” is the <hi type="italic">non plus ultra</hi> of vanity, - vanity in the highest degree. The double exclamation is followed by a statement which shows it to be the result of experience. “All is vain” - the whole (of the things, namely, which present themselves to us here below for our consideration and use) is vanity.
entries.f5001e4ddff6113ac113fa1dde562711efa6567e: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.3">Ecc 1:3</reference> <div eID="gen12195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12196" type="x-p"/> With this verse commences the proof for this exclamation and statement: “What profit hath a man of all his labour which he laboureth in under the sun?!” An interrogative exclamation, which leads to the conclusion that never anything right, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, real, enduring, satisfying, comes of it.יתרון, profit, synon. with <hi type="italic">Mothar</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.19">Ecc 3:19</reference>, is peculiar to this book (= Aram. יוּתרן). A primary form, יתרון, is unknown. The punctator Simson (Cod. 102a of the Leipzig University Lib.f. 5a) rightly blames those who use ויתּרון, in a liturgical hymn, of the Day of Atonement. The word signifies that which remains over, either, as here, clear gain, profit, or that which has the pre-eminence, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, superiority, precedence, or is the foremost. “Under the sun” is the designation of the earth peculiar to this book, - the world of men, which we are wont to call the sublunary world. שׁ has not the force of an accusative of manner, but of the obj. The author uses the expression, “Labour wherein I have laboured,” <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.19-Eccl.2.20">Ecc 2:19-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">Ecc 5:17</reference>, as Euripides, similarly, μοχθεῖν μόχθον. He now proceeds to justify the negative contained in the question, “What profit?”
entries.0466611689bb81d3251203f52573b06c6e497768: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">Ecc 1:4</reference> “One generation passeth away, and another generation cometh: and the earth remaineth for ev.” The meaning is not that the earth remains standing, and thus (Hitz.) approaches no limit (for what limit for it could be had in view?); it is by this very immoveable condition that it fulfils, according to the ancient notion, its destiny, Psa 119:90. The author rather intends to say that in this sphere nothing remains permanent as the fixed point around which all circles; generations pass away, others appear, and the earth is only the firm territory, the standing scene, of this ceaseless change. In reality, both things may be said of the earth: that it stands for ever without losing its place in the universe, and that it does not stand for ever, for it will be changed and become something else. But the latter thought, which appertains to the history of redemption, Psa 102:26., is remote from the Preacher; the stability of the earth appears to him only as the foil of the growth and decay everlastingly repeating themselves. Elster, in this fact, that the generations of men pass away, and that, on the contrary, the insensate earth under their feet remains, rightly sees something tragic, as Jerome had already done: <hi type="italic">Quid hac vanius vanitate, quam terram manere, quae hominum causa facta est, et hominem ipsum, terrae dominum, tam repente in pulverem dissolvi?</hi> The sun supplies the author with another figure. This, which he thinks of in contrast with the earth, is to him a second example of ceaseless change with perpetual sameness. As the generations of men come and go, so also does the sun.
entries.8ce8aff45610ea2099c2c5c93b649e74414bba51: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.5">Ecc 1:5</reference> “And the sun ariseth, the sun goeth down, and it hasteth (back) to its place, there to rise again.” It rises and sets again, but its setting is not a coming to rest; for from its place of resting in the west it must rise again in the morning in the east, hastening to fulfil its course. Thus Hitzig rightly, for he takes “there to rise again” as a relative clause; the words may be thus translated, but strictly taken, both participles stand on the same level; שׁואף (panting, hastening) is like בּא in <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">Ecc 1:4</reference>, the expression of the present, and זו that of the <hi type="italic">fut. instans: ibi</hi> (<hi type="italic">rursus</hi>) <hi type="italic">oriturus</hi>; the accentuation also treats the two partic. as co-ordinate, for <hi type="italic">Tiphcha</hi> separates more than <hi type="italic">Tebir</hi>; but it is inappropriate that it gives to ואל־ם the greater disjunctive <hi type="italic">Zakef Quaton</hi> (with <hi type="italic">Kadma</hi> going before). Ewald adopts this sequence of the accents, for he explains: the sun goes down, and that to its own place, viz., hastening back to it just by its going down, where, panting, it again ascends. But that the sun goes down to the place of its ascending, is a distorted thought. If “to its place” belongs to “goeth,” then it can refer only to the place of the going down, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Benjamin el-Nahawendi (Neubauer, <hi type="italic">Aus der Petersb. Bibl</hi>. p. 108) explains: “and that to its place,” viz., the place of the going down appointed for it by the Creator, with reference to <reference osisRef="Ps.104.19">Psa 104:19</reference>, “the sun knoweth his going down.” But the שׁם, which refers back to “its place,” opposes this interpretation; and the phrase שׁו cannot mean “panting, rising,” since שאף in itself does not signify to pant, but to snatch at, to long eagerly after anything, thus to strive, panting after it (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">Job 7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.131">Psa 119:131</reference>), which accords with the words “to its place,” but not with the act of rising. And how unnatural to think of the rising sun, which gives the impression of renewed youth, as panting! No, the panting is said of the sun that has set, which, during the night, and thus without rest by day and night, must turn itself back again to the east (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.7">Psa 19:7</reference>), there anew to commence its daily course. Thus also Rashi, the lxx, Syr., Targ., Jerome, Venet., and Luther. Instead of שׁו, Grätz would read שׁב אף, <hi type="italic">redit </hi>(<hi type="italic">atque</hi>)<hi type="italic">etiam</hi>; but שׁו is as characteristic of the Preacher’s manner of viewing the world as סובב וגו, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference></hi>, and ין, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">Ecc 1:8</reference></hi>. Thus much regarding the sun. Many old interpreters, recently Grätz, and among translators certainly the lxx, refer also <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference></hi> to the sun. The Targ. paraphrases the whole verse of the state of the sun by day and night, and at the spring and autumn equinox, according to which Rashi translates הרוּח, <hi type="italic">la volonté </hi>(<hi type="italic">du soleil</hi>). But along with the sun, the wind is also referred to as a third example of restless motion always renewing itself. The division of the verses is correct; <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference></hi> used of the sun would overload the figure, and the whole of <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference> therefore refers to the wind.
entries.0123f904924068b5293be25d048ead27c78ef02d: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference> “It goeth to the south, and turneth to the north; the wind goeth ever circling, and the wind returneth again on its circuits.” Thus designedly the verse is long-drawn and monotonous. It gives the impression of weariness. שׁב may be 3rd pret. with the force of an abstract present, but the relation is here different from that in 5 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, where the rising, setting, and returning stand together, and the two former lie backwards indeed against the latter; here, on the contrary, the circling motion and the return to a new beginning stand together on the same line; שׁב is thus a part., as the Syr. translates it. The participles represent continuance in motion. In <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.4">Ecc 1:4</reference> the subjects stand foremost, because the ever anew beginning motion belongs to the subject; in <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.5">Ecc 1:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference>, on the contrary, the pred. stands foremost, and the subject in <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.6">Ecc 1:6</reference> is therefore placed thus far back, because the first two pred. were not sufficient, but required a third for their completion. That the wind goes from the south (דּרום, R. דר, the region of the most intense light) to the north (צפון, R. צפן, the region of darkness), is not so exclusively true of it as it is of the sun that it goes from the east to the west; this expression requires the generalization “circling, circling goes the wind,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, turning in all directions here and there; for the repetition denotes that the circling movement exhausts all possibilities. The near defining part. which is subordinated to “goeth,” elsewhere is annexed by “and,” <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jonah.1.11">Jon 1:11</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>; here סבב סובב , in the sense of סביב  סביב, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.2">Eze 37:2</reference> (both times with <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> between the words), precedes. סביבה is here the <hi type="italic">n. actionis</hi> of סבב. And “on its circuits” is not to be taken adverbially: it turns back on its circuits, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it turns back on the same paths (Knobel and others), but על and שׁב are connected, as <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pro 26:11</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.19.7">Psa 19:7</reference> : the wind returns back to its circling movements to begin them anew (Hitzig). “The wind” is repeated (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.10">Ecc 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Ecc 4:1</reference>) according to the figure Epanaphora or Palindrome (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the <hi type="italic">Introd. to Isaiah</hi>, c. 40-66). To all regions of the heavens, to all directions of the compass, its movement is ceaseless, ever repeating itself anew; there is nothing permanent but the fluctuation, and nothing new but that the old always repeats itself. The examples are thoughtfully chosen and arranged. From the currents of air, the author now passes to streams of water.
entries.3af3e41c73bd3cda23373a63f07a776977802298: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.7">Ecc 1:7</reference> “All rivers run into the sea, and the sea becomes not full; to the place whence the rivers came, thither they always return again.” Instead of nehhárim, nehhalim was preferred, because it is the more general name for flowing waters, brooks, and rivers; נחל (from נחל, <hi type="italic">cavare</hi>), אפיק (from אפק, <hi type="italic">continere</hi>), and (Arab.) wadin (from the root-idea of stretching, extending), all three denote the channel or bed, and then the water flowing in it. The sentence, “all rivers run into the sea,” is consistent with fact. Manifestly the author does not mean that they all immediately flow thither; and by “the sea” he does not mean this or that sea; nor does he think, as the Targ. explains, of the earth as a ring (גּוּשׁפּנקא, Pers. angusht-bâne, properly “finger-guard”) surrounding the ocean: but the sea in general is meant, perhaps including also the ocean that is hidden. If we include this internal ocean, then the rivers which lose themselves in hollows, deserts, or inland lakes, which have no visible outlet, form no exception. But the expression refers first of all to the visible sea-basins, which gain no apparent increase by these masses of water being emptied into them: “the sea, it becomes not full;” איננּוּ (Mishn. אינו) has the reflex. pron., as at <reference osisRef="Exod.3.2">Exo 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.13.34">Lev 13:34</reference>, and elsewhere. If the sea became full, then there would be a real change; but this sea, which, as Aristophanes says (<hi type="italic">Clouds</hi>, 1294f.), οὐδὲν γίγνεται ἐπιῤῥηεόντων τῶν ποταμῶν πλείων, represents also the eternal sameness. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Lev.13.7">Lev 13:7</reference></hi>, Symm., Jer., Luther, and also Zöckler, translate שׁ in the sense of “from whence;” others, as Ginsburg, venture to take שׁם in the sense of משּׁם; both interpretations are linguistically inadmissible. <div eID="gen12196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12197" type="x-p"/> Generally the author does not mean to say that the rivers return to their sources, since the sea replenishes the fountains, but that where they once flow, they always for ever flow without changing their course, viz., into the all-devouring sea (Elst.); for the water rising out of the sea in vapour, and collecting itself in rain-clouds, fills the course anew, and the rivers flow on anew, for the old repeats itself in the same direction to the same end. מקום is followed by what is a virtual genitive (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.8">Psa 104:8</reference>); the accentuation rightly extends this only to הלכים; for אשׁר, according to its relation, signifies in itself <hi type="italic">ubi</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.39.20">Gen 39:20</reference>, and <hi type="italic">quo</hi>, Num 13:27; 1Ki 12:2 (never <hi type="italic">unde</hi>). שׁם, however, has after verbs of motion, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.22.27">Jer 22:27</reference> after שׁוב, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.6">1Sa 9:6</reference> after הלך, frequently the sense of שׁמּה. And שׁוּב with ל and the infin. signifies to do something again, Hos 11:9; <reference osisRef="Job.7.7">Job 7:7</reference>, thus: to the place whither the rivers flow, thither they flow again, <hi type="italic">eo rursus eunt</hi>. The author here purposely uses only participles, because although there is constant change, yet that which renews itself is ever the same. He now proceeds, after this brief but comprehensive induction of particulars, to that which is general.
entries.b5bce94d76af685c73cf588e8020cd2cfde3b788: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.8">Ecc 1:8</reference> “All things are in activity; no man can utter it; the eye is not satisfied with seeing, and the ear is not full with hearing.” All translators and interpreters who understand devarim here of words (lxx, Syr., and Targ.) go astray; for if the author meant to say that no words can describe this everlasting sameness with perpetual change, then he would have expressed himself otherwise than by “all words weary” (Ew., Elst., Hengst., and others); he ought at least to have said לריק יג. But also “all things are wearisome” (Knob., Hitz.), or “full of labour” (Zöck.), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, it is wearisome to relate them all, cannot be the meaning of the sentence; for יגע does not denote that which causes weariness, but that which suffers weariness (<reference osisRef="Deut.25.18">Deu 25:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.2">2Sa 7:2</reference>); and to refer the affection, instead of to the narrator, to that which is to be narrated, would be even for a poet too affected a <hi type="italic">quid pro quo</hi>. Rosenmüller essentially correctly: <hi type="italic">omnes res fatigantur h. e. in perpetua versantur vicissitudine, qua fatigantur quasi</hi>. But יגעים is not appropriately rendered by <hi type="italic">fatigantur</hi>; the word means, becoming wearied, or perfectly feeble, or also: wearying oneself (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.15">Ecc 10:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.12">Ecc 12:12</reference>), working with a strain on one’s strength, fatiguing oneself (cf.יגיע, that which is gained by labour, work). This is just what these four examples are meant to show, viz., that a restless activity reaching no visible conclusion and end, always beginning again anew, pervades the whole world-all things, he says, summarizing, are in labour, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, are restless, hastening on, giving the impression of fatigue. <div eID="gen12197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12198" type="x-p"/> Thus also in strict sequence of thought that which follows: this unrest in the outer world reflects itself in man, when he contemplates that which is done around him; human language cannot exhaust this coming and going, this growth and decay in constant circle, and the <hi type="italic">quodlibet</hi> is so great, that the eye cannot be satisfied with seeing, nor the ear with hearing; to the unrest of things without corresponds the unrest of the mind, which through this course, in these ever repeated variations, always bringing back the old again to view, is kept in ceaseless activity. The object to dǎbbēr is the totality of things. No words can comprehend this, no sensible perception exhaust it. That which is properly aimed at here is not the unsatisfiedness of the eyes (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.20">Pro 27:20</reference>), and generally of the mind, thus not the ever-new attractive power which appertains to the eye and the ear of him who observes, but the force with which the restless activity which surrounds us lays hold of and communicates itself to us, so that we also find no rest and contentment. With שׂבע, to be satisfied, of the eye, there is appropriately interchanged נמלא, used of the funnel-shaped ear, to be filled, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to be satisfied (as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.7">Ecc 6:7</reference>). The <hi type="italic">min</hi> connected with this latter word is explained by Zöck. after Hitz., “away from hearing,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, so that it may hear no more. This is not necessary. As saava' with its min may signify to be satisfied with anything, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.3">Ecc 6:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.19.22">Job 19:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.13">Psa 104:13</reference>; cf. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.2.6">Isa 2:6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Pih</hi>. <reference osisRef="Jer.51.34">Jer 51:34</reference>; Psa 127:5. Thus mishshemoa' is understood by all the old translators (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Targ. מלּמשׁמע), and thus also, perhaps, the author meant it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, and the ear is not filled (satisfied) with hearing; or yet more in accordance with the Heb. expression: there is not an eye, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, no eye is satisfied, etc., restlessly hastening, giving him who looks no rest, the world goes on in its circling course without revealing anything that is in reality new.
entries.36ea9c2f36b1e01ba490faf179614bf16dbd770f: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.9">Ecc 1:9</reference> “That which hath been is that which shall be, and that which is done is that which shall be done; and there is nothing new under the sun.” - The older form of the language uses only אשׁר instead of מה־שּׁ, in the sense of <hi type="italic">id quod</hi>, and in the sense of <hi type="italic">quid-quid</hi>, אשׁר כל (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.10">Ecc 6:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.24">Ecc 7:24</reference>); but mǎh is also used by it with the extinct force of an interrogative, in the sense of <hi type="italic">quodcunque</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.13.13">Job 13:13</reference>, <hi type="italic">aliquid</hi> (<hi type="italic">quidquam</hi>), <reference osisRef="Gen.39.8">Gen 39:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.9.13">Pro 9:13</reference>; and <hi type="italic">mi</hi> or <hi type="italic">mi asher</hi>, in the sense of <hi type="italic">quisquis</hi>, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.14">Exo 24:14</reference>; Exo 32:33. In שׁ הוא (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.42.14">Gen 42:14</reference>) are combined the meanings <hi type="italic">id </hi>(<hi type="italic">est</hi>)<hi type="italic">quod</hi> and <hi type="italic">idem </hi>(<hi type="italic">est</hi>)<hi type="italic">quod</hi>; hu is often the expression of the equality of two things, <reference osisRef="Job.3.19">Job 3:19</reference>, or of self-sameness, Psa 102:28. The double clause, quod f<hi type="italic">uit ... quod factum est</hi>, comprehends that which is done in the world of nature and of men-the natural and the historical. The bold clause, <hi type="italic">neque est quidquam novi sub sole</hi>, challenges contradiction; the author feels this, as the next verse shows.
entries.f03e2ef37729e061ef7a138ac37260875af382e4: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.10">Ecc 1:10</reference> “Is there anything whereof it may be said: See, this is new? - it was long ago through the ages (aeons) which have been before us.” The Semit. substantive verb ישׁ (Assyr. isu) has here the force of a hypothetical antecedent: supposing that there is a thing of which one might say, etc. The זה, with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, belongs as subject, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.27">Ecc 7:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.29">Ecc 7:29</reference> as object, to that which follows. כּבר (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., List, p. 193) properly denotes length or greatness of time (as כּברה, length of way). The ל of לע is that of measure: this “long ago” measured (Hitz.) after infinitely long periods of time. מלּ, <hi type="italic">ante nos</hi>, follows the usage of מלּף, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.26">Isa 41:26</reference>, and l|paa', Jdg 1:10, etc.; the past time is spoken of as that which was before, for it is thought of as the beginning of the succession of time (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Orelli, <hi type="italic">Synon. der Zeit u. Ewigkeit</hi>, p. 14f.). The singular היה may also be viewed as pred. of a <hi type="italic">plur. inhumanus</hi> in order; but in connection, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.7">Ecc 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.9">Ecc 2:9</reference> (Gesen. §147, An. 2), it is more probable that it is taken as a neut. verb. That which newly appears has already been, but had been forgotten; for generations come and generations go, and the one forgets the other.
entries.9629496113ac7ebe827a2428d81ff21e06b9fc03: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.11">Ecc 1:11</reference> “There is no remembrance of ancestors; and also of the later ones who shall come into existence, there will be no remembrance for them with those who shall come into existence after them.” With זכּרון (with <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi>) there is also זכרון, the more common form by our author, in accordance with the usage of his age; Gesen., Elst., and others regard it here and at <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.16">Ecc 2:16</reference> as constr., and thus לרא as virtually object-gen. (Jerome, <hi type="italic">non est priorum memoria</hi>); but such refinements of the old <hi type="italic">syntaxis ornata</hi> are not to be expected in our author: he changes (according to the traditional punctuation) here the initial sound, as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">Ecc 1:17</reference> the final sound, to <hi type="italic">oth</hi> and <hi type="italic">uth</hi>. אין ל is the contrast of היה ל: to attribute to one, to become partaker of. The use of the expression, “for them,” gives emphasis to the statement. “With those who shall come after,” points from the generation that is future to a remoter future, cf. Gen 33:2. The <hi type="italic">Kametz</hi> of the prep. is that of the recompens. art.; cf. Num 2:31, where it denotes “the last” among the four hosts; for there הא is meant of the last in order, as here it is meant of the remotely future time.
entries.7e71f5f6956d8f281a849411d61fb413b862e7cf: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.12">Ecc 1:12</reference> “I, Koheleth, have been king over Israel in Jerusalem.” That of the two possible interpretations of הייתי, “I have become” and “I have been,” not the former (Grätz), but the latter, is to be here adopted, has been already shown. We translate better by “I have been” - for the verb here used is a pure perfect - than by “I was” (Ew., Elst., Hengst., Zöck.), with which Bullock (<hi type="italic">Speaker’s Comm.</hi>, vol. IV, 1873) compares the expression <hi type="italic">Quand j'étois roi !</hi> which was often used by Louis XIV towards the end of his life. But here the expression is not a cry of complaint, like the “<hi type="italic">fuimus Troes</hi>,” but a simple historical statement, by which the Preacher of the vanity of all earthly things here introduces himself, - it is Solomon, resuscitated by the author of the book, who here looks back on his life as king. “Israel” is the whole of Israel, and points to a period before the division of the kingdom; a king over Judah alone would not so describe himself. Instead of “king על (over) Israel,” the old form of the language uses frequently simply “king of Israel,” although also the former expression is sometimes found; cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.26">1Sa 15:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.23">2Sa 19:23</reference>; 1Ki 11:37. He has been king, - king over a great, peaceful, united people; king in Jerusalem, the celebrated, populous, highly-cultivated city, - and thus placed on an elevation having the widest survey, and having at his disposal whatever can make a man happy; endowed, in particular, with all the means of gaining knowledge, which accorded with the disposition of his heart searching after wisdom (cf. 1Ki 3:9-11; 1Ki 5:9). <div eID="gen12198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12199" type="x-p"/> But in his search after worldly knowledge he found no satisfaction.
entries.de333c606486295d24f015a1c7695ea15143c417: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ecc 1:13</reference> “And I gave my heart to seek and to hold survey with wisdom over all that is done under the sun: a sore trouble it is which God has given to the children of men to be exercised therewith.” The synonyms דּרשׁ(to seek) and תּוּר (to hold survey over) do not represent a lower and a higher degree of search (Zöck.), but two kinds of searching: one penetrating in depth, the other going out in extent; for the former of these verbs (from the root-idea of grinding, testing) signifies to investigate an object which one already has in hand, to penetrate into it, to search into it thoroughly; and the latter verb (from the root-idea of moving round about)<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., the investigation of these roots (Assyr. utîr, he brought back) in Ethé’s <hi type="italic">Schlafgemach der Phantasie</hi>, pp. 86-89.</note> signifies to hold a survey, - look round in order to bring that which is unknown, or not comprehensively known, within the sphere of knowledge, and thus has the meaning of bǎkkēsh, one going the rounds. It is the usual word for the exploring of a country, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the acquiring personal knowledge of its as yet unknown condition; the passing over to an intellectual search is peculiar to the Book of Koheleth, as it has the phrase ל לב נתן, <hi type="italic">animum advertere</hi>, or <hi type="italic">applicare ad aliquid</hi>, in common only with Dan 10:12. The beth of bahhochemah is that of the instrument; wisdom must be the means (<hi type="italic">organon</hi>) of knowledge in this searching and inquiry. With על is introduced the sphere into which it extends. Grotius paraphrases: <hi type="italic">Historiam animalium et satorum diligentissime inquisivi</hi>. But נעשׂה does not refer to the world of nature, but to the world of men; only within this can anything be said of actions, only this has a proper history. But that which offers itself for research and observation there, brings neither joy nor contentment. Hitzig refers הוּא to human activity; but it relates to the research which has this activity as its object, and is here, on that account, called “a sore trouble,” because the attainment and result gained by the laborious effort are of so unsatisfactory a nature. Regarding ענין, which here goes back to ענה ב, to fatigue oneself, to trouble oneself with anything, and then to be engaged with it. The words ענין רע would mean trouble of an evil nature (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Psa 78:49</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.6.24">Pro 6:24</reference>); but better attested is the reading ענין רע “a sore trouble.” הוּא is the subj., as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1">Ecc 2:1</reference> and elsewhere; the author uses it also in expressions where it is pred. And as frequently as he uses <hi type="italic">asher</hi> and שׁ, so also, when form and matter commend it, he uses the scheme of the attributive clause (elliptical relative clause), as here (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ecc 3:16</reference>), where certainly, in conformity with the old style, נתנו was to be used.
entries.c0755f56590b0a034767cd22bb7acbce6f12a157: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.14">Ecc 1:14</reference> <div eID="gen12199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12200" type="x-p"/> He adduces proof of the wearisomeness of this work of research: “I saw all the works that are done under the sun; and, behold, all is vanity and striving after the wind.” The point of the sentence lies in והנּה = וארא וה, so that thus <hi type="italic">raïthi</hi> is the expression of the parallel fact (circumst. perfect). The result of his seeing, and that, as he has said <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.13">Ecc 1:13</reference>, of a by no means superficial and limited seeing, was a discovery of the fleeting, unsubstantial, fruitless nature of all human actions and endeavours. They had, as <hi type="italic">hevel</hi> expresses, not reality in them; and also, as denoted by reuth ruahh (the lxx render well by προαίρεσις πνεύματος), they had no actual consequences, no real issue. Hos 12:1 also says: “Ephraim feedeth on wind,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, follows after, as the result of effort obtains, the wind, roěh ruahh; but only in the Book of Koheleth is this sentence transformed into an abstract <hi type="italic">terminus technicus</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under Reth).
entries.9ecd04e2d1f26e6bdefa5cffe34fa62e5b3a91c5: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.15">Ecc 1:15</reference> <div eID="gen12200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12201" type="x-p"/> The judgment contained in the words, “vanity and a striving after the wind,” is confirmed: “That which is crooked cannot become straight; and a deficit cannot be numerable,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, cannot be taken into account (thus Theod., after the Syro-Hex.), as if as much were present as is actually wanting; for, according to the proverb, “Where there is nothing, nothing further is to be counted.” Hitzig thinks, by that which is crooked and wanting, according to <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13">Ecc 7:13</reference>, of the divine order of the world: that which is unjust in it, man cannot alter; its wants he cannot complete. But the preceding statement refers only to labour under the sun, and to philosophical research and observation directed thereto. This places before the eyes of the observer irregularities and wants, brings such irregularities and wants to his consciousness, - which are certainly partly brought about and destined by God, but for the most part are due to the transgressions of man himself, - and what avails the observer the discovery and investigation? - he has only lamentation over it, for with all his wisdom he can bring no help. Instead of לתקן (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under תקן), לתקן was to be expected. However, the old language also formed intransitive infinitives with transitive modification of the final vowels, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, יבשׁ, etc. (cf. ישׁון, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.11">Ecc 5:11</reference>). <div eID="gen12201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12202" type="x-p"/> Having now gained such a result in his investigation and research by means of wisdom, he reaches the conclusion that wisdom itself is nothing.
entries.bef230e48743bdd08aab3aeff28960d3420d0e54: <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.16-Eccl.1.18">Ecc 1:16-18</reference> “I have communed with mine own heart, saying: Lo, I have gained great and always greater wisdom above all who were before me over Jerusalem; and my heart hath seen wisdom and knowledge in fulness. And I gave my heart to know what was in wisdom and knowledge, madness and folly - I have perceived that this also is a grasping after the wind.” The evidence in which he bears witness to himself that striving after wisdom and knowledge brings with it no true satisfaction, reaches down to the close of <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.17">Ecc 1:17</reference>; ידעתּי is the conclusion which is aimed at. The manner of expression is certainly so far involved, as he speaks of his heart to his heart what it had experienced, and to what he had purposely directed it. The אני leads us to think that a king speaks, for whom it is appropriate to write a capital <hi type="italic">I</hi>, or to multiply it into <hi type="italic">we</hi>; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding this “I,” more pleonastic than emphatic, subordinated to its verb. <div eID="gen12202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12203" type="x-p"/> It is a question whether עם־לבּי, after the phrase (את) עם דּבּר, is meant of speaking with any one, <hi type="italic">colloqui</hi>, or of the place of speaking, as in “thou shalt consider in thine heart,” <reference osisRef="Deut.8.5">Deu 8:5</reference>, it is used of the place of consciousness; cf. <reference osisRef="Job.15.9">Job 15:9</reference>, (עמּדי) עמּי היה = σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ, and what is said in my <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 134, regarding συνείδησις, consciousness, and συμμαρτυρεῖν. בּלבּי, interchanging with עם־לבּי, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1">Ecc 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.15">Ecc 2:15</reference>, commends the latter meaning: in my heart (lxx, Targ., Jerome, Luther); but the cogn. expressions, medabběrěth ǎl-libbah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.13">1Sa 1:13</reference>, and ledabbēr ěl-libbi, <reference osisRef="Gen.24.45">Gen 24:45</reference>, suggest as more natural the former rendering, viz., as of a dialogue, which is expressed by the <hi type="italic">Gr. Venet.</hi> (more distinctly than by Aquila, Symm., and Syr.): διείλεγμαι ἐγὼ ξὺν τῇ καρδίᾳ μου. Also לאמר, occurring only here in the Book of Koheleth, brings it near that the following oratio directa is directed to the heart, as it also directly assumes the form of an address, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.1">Ecc 2:1</reference>, after בלבי. The expression, הג הך, “to make one’s wisdom great,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, “to gain great wisdom,” is without a parallel; for the words, הג תו, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.29">Isa 28:29</reference>, quoted by Hitzig, signify to show and attest truly useful (beneficial) knowledge in a noble way. The annexed והו refers to the continued increase made to the great treasure already possessed (cf. <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.9">Ecc 2:9</reference> and 1Ki 10:7). The <hi type="italic">al</hi> connected therewith signifies, “above” (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.26">Gen 49:26</reference>) all those who were over Jerusalem before me. This is like the sarrâni âlik maḥrija, “the kings who were my predecessors,” which was frequently used by the Assyrian kings. The Targumist seeks to accommodate the words to the actual Solomon by thus distorting them: “above all the wise men who have been in Jerusalem before me,” as if the word in the text were בירושלם,<note placement="foot">In F. the following note is added: “Several Codd. have, erroneously, birushalam instead of al-jerushalam.” Kennicott counts about 60 such Codd. It stands thus also in J; and at first it thus stood in H, but was afterwards corrected to al-yerushalam. Cf. Elias Levita’s <hi type="italic">Masoreth hamasoreth</hi>, II 8, at the end.</note> as it is indeed found in several Codd., and according to which also the lxx, Syr., Jerome, and the Venet. translate. Rather than think of the wise (הכּימיּא), we are led to think of all those who from of old stood at the head of the Israelitish community. But there must have been well-known great men with whom Solomon measures himself, and these could not be such dissimilarly great men as the Canaanitish kings to the time of Melchizedek; and since the Jebusites, even under Saul, were in possession of Zion, and Jerusalem was for the first time completely subdued by David (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.7">2Sa 5:7</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.15.63">Jos 15:63</reference>), it is evident that only one predecessor of Solomon in the office of ruler over Jerusalem can be spoken of, and that here an anachronism lies before us, occasioned by the circumstance that the <hi type="italic">Salomo revivivus</hi>, who has behind him the long list of kings whom in truth he had before him, here speaks. <div eID="gen12203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12204" type="x-p"/> Regarding היה אשׁר, qu'il y uet, for היו אשׁר, <hi type="italic">qui furent</hi>, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Eccl.1.10">Ecc 1:10</reference></hi>. The seeing here ascribed to the heart (here = νοῦς, <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 249) is meant of intellectual observation and apprehension; for “all perception, whether it be mediated by the organs of sense or not (as prophetic observing and contemplating), comprehends all, from mental discernment down to suffering, which veils itself in unconsciousness, and the Scripture designates it as a seeing” (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. 234); the Book of Koheleth also uses the word ראה of every kind of human experience, bodily or mental, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.24">Ecc 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.17">Ecc 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.6">Ecc 6:6</reference>; Ecc 9:9. It is commonly translated: “My heart saw much wisdom and knowledge” (thus <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Ewald); but that is contrary to the gram. structure of the sentence (Ew. §287 <hi type="italic">c</hi>). The adject. harbēh<note placement="foot">Regarding the form הרבה, which occurs once (<reference osisRef="Jer.42.2">Jer 42:2</reference>), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Ew. §240c.</note> is always, and by Koheleth also, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.7">Ecc 2:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.6">Ecc 5:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.16">Ecc 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.11">Ecc 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.18">Ecc 9:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.8">Ecc 11:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.9">Ecc 12:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.12">Ecc 12:12</reference>, placed after its subst.; thus it is here adv., as at <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">Ecc 5:19</reference>; Ecc 7:16. Rightly the Venet.: ἡ καρδία μου τεθέαται κατὰ πολὺ σοφίαν καί γνῶσιν <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> signifies, properly, solidity, compactness; and then, like πυκνότης, mental ability, secular wisdom; and, generally, solid knowledge of the true and the right. Dǎǎth is connected with <hi type="italic">chokma</hi> here and at <reference osisRef="Isa.33.6">Isa 33:6</reference>, as at <reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom 11:33</reference>, γνῶσις is with σοφία. Baumggarten-Crusius there remarks that σοφία refers to the general ordering of things, γνῶσις to the determination of individual things; and Harless, that σοφία is knowledge which proposes the right aim, and γνῶσις that which finds the right means thereto. In general, we may say that <hi type="italic">chokma</hi> is the fact of a powerful knowledge of the true and the right, and the property which arises out of this intellectual possession; but dǎǎth is knowledge penetrating into the depth of the essence of things, by which wisdom is acquired and in which wisdom establishes itself.
